title: Policy Learning with a Natural Language Action Space: A Causal Approach
venue_date: CONFIRMED (id and title match). arXiv preprint, submitted 24 Feb 2025; cs.CL; no published venue found (searched ACL Anthology / proceedings — preprint only as of 2026-09). Authors: Bohan Zhang, Yixin Wang, Paramveer S. Dhillon (Michigan).
what_it_does: Proposes an explicitly causal framework for multi-stage decision-making where the action at each stage IS a piece of natural language and the outcome is only observed after the whole sequence. It estimates a Dynamic Treatment Regime by fitting a stage-wise Q-function as a single text classifier over (history, action) text, citing Murphy and Robins for the DTR/optimal-Q machinery. It then recovers the optimal language action by gradient ascent on the action's embedding and decodes it back to text with a 'Repeat: [TEXT]' T5 trick plus GPT-2-perplexity/beam selection — i.e. a generative text policy optimized against the learned causal critic. Evaluated on three two-stage domains: Intern Health Study mental-health intervention refinement (synthetic interventions grounded in real PHQ-9 trajectories), DIALOCONAN hate-speech counter-speech, and Yelp/Amazon sentiment transfer.
overlap_with_us: This is the single most dangerous paper: it already claims the 'language actions as sequential treatments + DTR/Q-learning + generate text against the causal critic' package. It covers our (i) in weak form (DTR framing of language-valued interventions, history as the conditioning set), our (ii) minus the STOP action (stage-wise optimal Q, but a fixed 2-stage horizon, no termination decision), and our (iii) essentially in full (gradient ascent on the critic's input embedding, decoded to text — a generative policy trained against a causal critic). A hostile reviewer cites this as 'already done'. Our actual daylight: (a) their treatment is the ASSISTANT's refinement action on a target text, not the USER-side prompt/feedback in a real human-LLM dialogue; (b) they do not state or defend sequential ignorability, and per the full text they never use g-estimation, blip/structural nested mean models, doubly-robust or DR-learner estimation — the 'causal' content is essentially Q-learning on text with a citation to Murphy; (c) no STOP/termination action; (d) no inference (no standard errors, no non-regularity handling at the boundary where blips vanish). We must lead with identification + blip-function estimation + STOP, and cite this as the closest prior work, not discover it at review time. Note: search snippets describing it as a 'novel causal framework ... enabling data-efficient policy learning' are accurate to the abstract but overstate the rigor of the causal content relative to the body.

title: What is the Causal Effect of a Conversation? Estimands and Inference in AI Mediated Conversations
venue_date: CONFIRMED (id and title match). arXiv preprint, submitted 3 Jul 2026; stat.ME (Statistics > Methodology); 42 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Authors: Adriane Fresh, Aiden Shin.
what_it_does: A methodological paper arguing that when researchers use conversations (increasingly AI-generated ones) as treatments, 'the conversation' is not one causal object but several: assignment to a conversational condition, the conversational POLICY, the opening message, individual messages within the conversation, realized conversational features, and the complete realized conversation. It shows that randomizing assignment identifies only the first of these, and that the finer-grained estimands require sequential assumptions plus representations of conversational history. It reports that in multi-turn AI chat experiments with randomization only at the policy/opening-prompt level, residual associations between pre-treatment respondent traits and realized message features survive conditioning on observed history — i.e. sequential ignorability empirically fails, so message- and feature-level effects are not identified without explicit message-level intervention.
overlap_with_us: This is the identification kill-shot, and it pre-empts our conceptual contribution (i). It already builds the taxonomy of causal objects in multi-turn AI conversation that we were going to build, and it gives a hostile reviewer a citable, 2026, stat.ME argument that our central estimand — the effect of the turn-t user prompt given history — is NOT identified from observational or policy-randomized conversation logs, because the conversation history is jointly generated by the user and the model and observed history does not suffice for sequential ignorability. Every claim we make about 'conversation history as the time-varying confounder' has to answer this paper directly. Two live responses: (a) design — micro-randomize at the turn level (SMART/MRT-style prompt randomization), which this paper implicitly points to as the fix, making randomized turn-level intervention a design contribution rather than an assumption; (b) be explicit that the blip/Q target is a policy-class-restricted estimand. Do not frame our work as 'first to define these estimands' — that claim is gone.

title: ArCHer: Training Language Model Agents via Hierarchical Multi-Turn RL
venue_date: CONFIRMED (id and title match). arXiv, submitted 29 Feb 2024; cs.LG; published at ICML 2024 (also on OpenReview). Authors: Yifei Zhou, Andrea Zanette, Jiayi Pan, Sergey Levine, Aviral Kumar.
what_it_does: Builds a hierarchical RL framework for fine-tuning LLMs over multi-turn interaction with delayed, sparse rewards. It runs two algorithms in parallel: a high-level, off-policy, value-based learner that aggregates reward across UTTERANCES (a turn-level Q/value function trained with TD backups, implemented with a RoBERTa-style critic), and a low-level on-policy token-level policy-gradient learner that optimizes the token policy within a turn against that high-level value function. Reports ~100x sample efficiency over PPO and better asymptotic performance than off-policy baselines, scaling to 7B.
overlap_with_us: This is the 'it's just X with causal language bolted on' citation for components (ii) and (iii). Our turn-level blip/Q critic is, computationally, ArCHer's utterance-level critic; our 'generative prompt policy trained against the causal critic' is ArCHer's token-level actor trained against the high-level value function. A reviewer will say: the architecture, the credit assignment across turns, and the actor-critic training are all here, and 'time-varying treatment / time-varying confounder / blip function' is a relabeling of (action / state / advantage). Our defense has to be things RL does not give: identification from observational or micro-randomized logs rather than online rollouts, a target of inference with valid confidence intervals on the blip parameters, doubly-robust/g-estimation-based estimation under confounding, and non-regularity at the STOP boundary. If we cannot articulate an estimand-and-inference contribution beyond 'we get a better policy', this paper sinks us. Combine with arXiv:2405.14655 (Shani et al., Multi-turn RLHF, NeurIPS 2024) and arXiv:2512.04601 (Natural Language Actor-Critic, Dec 2025 / v2 Feb 2026) — both also do multi-turn credit assignment in language space.

title: Causal Inference with Generative Artificial Intelligence: Application to Texts as Treatments
venue_date: CONFIRMED (id matches; note the title on arXiv is 'Causal Inference with Generative Artificial Intelligence...', while some search results render it as 'Causal Representation Learning with Generative Artificial Intelligence: Application to Texts as Treatments' — likely an earlier version's title, so cite the current one). arXiv, v1 1 Oct 2024, v5 revised 11 Jun 2026; stat.AP. Authors: Kosuke Imai, Kentaro Nakamura.
what_it_does: Addresses causal inference when the treatment is an unstructured, high-dimensional text. Instead of learning a causal representation from observational text (Egami/Pryzant-style), they have an LLM GENERATE the treatment texts and use the LLM's internal representations as the deconfounding/feature layer, which they argue removes the need to learn representations from data. They give nonparametric identification conditions for the ATE of text treatments, an estimation strategy engineered to avoid overlap violations, and double machine learning asymptotics; they extend to human-perception mediators via an instrumental-variables approach.
overlap_with_us: This is the citation that pre-empts our claim to 'identify causal effects of language-valued interventions'. For the SINGLE-period case, identification of text-valued treatments with overlap handling and DML inference is already solved by a top-tier stats team, and v5 is dated June 2026 so it is current. A reviewer will demand that our contribution be specifically the SEQUENTIAL extension (time-varying text treatments, time-varying confounding by history, g-formula/blip decomposition) and will not credit us for anything in the static case. Pair with arXiv:2607.26309 ('The Confounder Trap: Treatment-Encoding Representations in Causal Inference with Text', Jul 2026, seen in search but NOT independently verified by me) which shows that rich text representations can encode treatment and manufacture overlap violations — a direct methodological hazard for our history-as-confounder embeddings.

title: Optimizing Prompts for Large Language Models: A Causal Approach
venue_date: CONFIRMED (id and title match; 2602 = Feb 2026, and it resolves correctly). arXiv, submitted 2 Feb 2026; no venue listed. Authors: Wei Chen, Yanbin Fang, Shuran Fu, Fasheng Xu, Xuan Wei.
what_it_does: Proposes Causal Prompt Optimization (CPO), reframing automatic prompt optimization as causal estimation. Stage 1 learns an OFFLINE CAUSAL REWARD MODEL by applying Double Machine Learning to semantic embeddings of prompts and queries, explicitly to strip out confounding by query attributes — their stated motivation is that existing dynamic APO methods rely on reward models that are 'fundamentally correlational, confounding prompt effectiveness with query characteristics'. Stage 2 uses that debiased reward to drive a cheap search for per-query prompts without online evaluation. Evaluated on math reasoning, visualization and data-analytics benchmarks; gains concentrated on hard queries, with a cost argument about moving evaluation offline.
overlap_with_us: Dangerous because it is recent (Feb 2026) and it already owns the exact rhetorical move we planned to open with — 'prompt-quality reward models are correlational, we make them causal' — and it already implements the debiased (DML) critic for prompts. It is single-turn/per-query, with no history, no sequential confounding, no regime, no STOP, so it does not scoop our sequential contribution; but it means our novelty framing cannot be 'prompt optimization should be causal' (taken) and must be 'prompt optimization over a HORIZON, where the confounder is generated by the prior turns'. Expect a reviewer to ask why our critic is not just CPO's causal reward model applied per turn — we need the answer that per-turn DML on a history-generated confounder is biased for the sequential blip and requires g-estimation/sequential-DR.

title: CaRT: Teaching LLM Agents to Know When They Know Enough
venue_date: CONFIRMED (id and title match). arXiv, submitted 9 Oct 2025; no venue listed on the abs page. Authors: Grace Liu, Yuxiao Qu, Jeff Schneider, Aarti Singh, Aviral Kumar.
what_it_does: Formalizes the problem of an agent that gathers information over multiple rounds and must decide WHEN TO STOP gathering and act, to avoid overthinking or derailing. CaRT fine-tunes an LLM on COUNTERFACTUAL PAIRS of trajectories — one where termination is appropriate and a minimally perturbed one where it is not — and trains the model to verbalize the rationale for the termination decision. Instantiated on interactive medical diagnosis and math problem solving; improves information-gathering efficiency and task success over other fine-tuning baselines. It is supervised fine-tuning on counterfactual pairs, not RL and not formal causal inference.
overlap_with_us: Direct threat to our component (ii)'s headline novelty, the STOP action, and it is doubly awkward because it uses the word 'counterfactual' for minimally-perturbed trajectory pairs — a reviewer skimming both will say our STOP contribution is CaRT with DTR vocabulary. What CaRT does NOT do: no potential-outcomes estimand for stopping, no value-based comparison of stop-vs-continue (no blip at the terminal decision), no handling of confounding in logged trajectories, and no inference. Our genuine contribution is that STOP is the decision where the optimal-regime blip is exactly zero, i.e. the non-regular/boundary case where naive plug-in Q-learning inference fails — that is a real statistical contribution CaRT cannot claim. Also compare arXiv:2410.13788 ('Modeling Future Conversation Turns to Teach LLMs to Ask Clarifying Questions', seen in search, NOT independently verified) on the ask-vs-answer decision.

title: Multi-turn Reinforcement Learning from Preference Human Feedback
venue_date: CONFIRMED (id and title match). arXiv v1 23 May 2024, v2 2 Dec 2024; published at NeurIPS 2024 (proceedings.neurips.cc poster 93434; the proceedings page renders the title as '...with Preference Human Feedback'). Authors: Shani, Rosenberg, Cassel, Lang, Calandriello, Zipori, Noga, Keller, Piot, Szpektor, Hassidim, Matias, Munos (Google DeepMind).
what_it_does: Extends RLHF from single-turn to preferences over two complete MULTI-TURN conversations, arguing that turn-level preference emulation cannot support planning toward a long-term goal. Introduces a mirror-descent-based policy optimization algorithm (MTPO) with a proof of convergence to a Nash equilibrium of the preference game in the tabular setting, plus a deep actor-critic instantiation. Validated in an 'Education Dialogue' environment (teacher agent teaching a student environment a topic), where it beats RLHF baselines.
overlap_with_us: Reinforces the ArCHer critique with a NeurIPS-published pedigree: multi-turn credit assignment for conversation, with trajectory-level (delayed) feedback and a critic, is established territory at the top venues. A reviewer will use this plus ArCHer to argue that the 'learn an optimal adaptive prompting regime' half of our project is an RL problem already well served, and that our value-add must be identification/inference from non-interactive data rather than policy quality. Note it optimizes the ASSISTANT's policy under simulated interaction, not the user-side prompt as a treatment, and it has no confounding story — that is our room.

title: Natural Language Actor-Critic: Scalable Off-Policy Learning in Language Space
venue_date: CONFIRMED (id and title match). arXiv v1 4 Dec 2025, v2 2 Feb 2026; cs.LG, cs.CL; 21 pages. Authors: Joey Hong, Kang Liu, Zhan Ling, Jiecao Chen, Sergey Levine.
what_it_does: Trains LLM agents off-policy with a critic whose output is natural language rather than a scalar: NLAC's generative LLM critic explains WHY an action is suboptimal, and the actor is improved from that textual signal without policy gradients. Motivated by the noisiness of trajectory-level rewards over long horizons and by the difficulty of exploring in an open-ended language action space. Results on a mixture of reasoning, web browsing, and tool-use-with-dialogue tasks. No causal framing.
overlap_with_us: Occupies the phrase 'critic over language actions, trained off-policy, used to improve a generative policy' — which is our component (iii) minus the causal estimand. A hostile reviewer pairs it with ArCHer to argue the actor-critic-in-language-space design space is saturated and that 'causal critic' is a renaming. Our distinguishing claim must be that our critic estimates a well-defined blip/contrast identified from logged data under stated assumptions and carries uncertainty, whereas NLAC's critic is an uncalibrated verbal judge.

title: Dynamic Policy Induction for Adaptive Prompt Optimization: Bridging the Efficiency-Accuracy Gap via Lightweight Reinforcement Learning
venue_date: CONFIRMED (id and title match). arXiv, submitted 28 Sep 2025; cs.LG/cs.AI/cs.CL; 13 pages; no venue listed. Author: Jiexi Xu.
what_it_does: Introduces the Prompt Policy Network (PPN), a small external network that chooses among prompting strategies (Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, CoT, Self-Consistency) per input, formalized as a SINGLE-STEP MDP and trained with PPO under a resource-explicit reward. Reports up to 61.5% token-cost reduction versus Self-Consistency at competitive accuracy on arithmetic reasoning, framed as an efficiency-accuracy Pareto result.
overlap_with_us: Weak on substance — single-step MDP, discrete strategy menu, no history, no confounding, no text generation — but it is rhetorically useful to a hostile reviewer as evidence that 'learn a policy that adaptively chooses the prompt, including whether to spend more turns' is a crowded, already-published idea, and its cost-aware reward is a cheap stand-in for our STOP action's cost of continuing. Cite it ourselves to draw the contrast (single-step strategy selection vs. sequential language-valued treatment with confounding) rather than let a reviewer produce it.

title: Controllable User Simulation
venue_date: arXiv preprint (cs.AI), submitted 12 May 2026. Authors: Guy Tennenholtz, Ofer Meshi, Amir Globerson, Uri Shalit, Jihwan Jeong, Craig Boutilier (Google DeepMind + Technion)
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] The paper formalizes controllable user simulation as a CAUSAL INFERENCE problem, so that a simulated user can be used to evaluate a new (counterfactual) agent policy rather than only replay logged conversations. Its central technical claim is that ordinary SFT-trained user simulators suffer 'look-ahead bias' that breaks causal consistency: the simulator's next user turn leaks information about the future of the logged trajectory, and as a result the variance of evaluation metrics 'explodes geometrically' when the agent policy is changed — they call this 'controllability collapse'. They propose three fixes (a priori controls, step-wise dynamic controls, and direct policy-conditioned learning) and claim the causally-grounded simulators eliminate look-ahead bias, preserve natural variance and generalize zero-shot to unseen agent behaviors. Note Uri Shalit is a causal-inference author, so the causal machinery here is real and not decorative.
overlap_with_us: This is the most dangerous paper I found. It attacks exactly our identification layer (i), from the simulator side: the conversation history is the time-varying state, the agent's turn is the intervention, and the 'look-ahead bias' they describe IS the g-computation/sequential-ignorability violation we would have to argue about when we use a user simulator or a learned behavior model to identify blip/Q functions. If we ever justify our estimands via a simulated user or a learned response model, a reviewer will ask why we are not just doing their thing. Differences we must own: (a) they intervene on the ASSISTANT policy and simulate the USER, we do the mirror image (user-side prompt is the treatment); (b) they are about evaluation/simulation fidelity, not about identifying blip effects of language-valued treatments or learning an optimal regime; (c) no STOP action, no regime optimization, no generative policy trained against a causal critic. We should cite this as the closest causal treatment of multi-turn human-LLM interaction and position our blip/Q identification as the estimation counterpart to their simulation counterpart.

title: Prompt-R1: Collaborative Automatic Prompting Framework via End-to-end Reinforcement Learning
venue_date: arXiv preprint (cs.CL), v1 2 Nov 2025, latest v9 16 Apr 2026. Authors: Wenjin Liu, Haoran Luo, Xueyuan Lin, Haoming Liu, Tiesunlong Shen, Jiapu Wang, Rui Mao, Erik Cambria
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] A small-scale LLM is trained, end-to-end with RL, to REPLACE THE USER: at each turn it reads the original question plus the accumulated interaction history and emits the next prompt to a large frozen LLM, which does the reasoning. A 'dual-constrained reward' scores correctness, generation quality and reasoning accuracy. It is plug-and-play across different large backbones for both inference and training. The abstract/page does not describe an explicit STOP/terminate action, and there is no causal-identification content — it is straight multi-turn policy-gradient on simulated user turns.
overlap_with_us: This is the plain-RL version of our component (iii) and, implicitly, (ii): a learned generative policy over user-side prompts, conditioned on conversation history, optimized for final task quality. It already occupies the headline 'learn what to say next to the model, as a policy not a heuristic'. What it does NOT have: any causal estimand (no blip/Q identification, no time-varying-confounding argument, no off-policy/offline identification from logged human conversations — it trains online against a live large LLM), no explicit STOP action, no notion of optimal adaptive regime with inference/uncertainty. Our framing must lead with identification + STOP + offline logged human data, and cite Prompt-R1 as the purely-optimization baseline our causal critic is meant to improve on.

title: Grounded in Reality: Learning and Deploying Proactive LLM from Offline Logs (the 'Learn-to-Ask' framework)
venue_date: arXiv:2510.25441 [cs.CL], submitted 29 Oct 2025, 27 pages. Authors: Fei Wei, Daoyuan Chen, Ce Wang, Yilun Huang, Yushuo Chen, Xuchen Pan, Yaliang Li, Bolin Ding (Alibaba)
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Learns a proactive dialogue policy (what to ask next) purely from OFFLINE expert interaction logs, with no user simulator. The trick is to exploit 'the observed future of each expert trajectory' to infer dense reward signals, which lets them reduce a long-horizon offline RL problem to a sequence of supervised learning tasks. The learned model emits structured tuples covering both WHAT to ask and WHEN TO STOP ASKING. They add an Automated Grader Calibration pipeline for LLM-judge reward noise, and report deployment of models up to 32B in a live medical AI service. No causal/counterfactual/confounding vocabulary anywhere.
overlap_with_us: Directly occupies (ii): an adaptive question-asking regime WITH a learned stop rule, learned offline from logged multi-turn human interaction. Their 'exploit the observed future of each expert trajectory' is, informally, exactly the hindsight/pseudo-outcome move that blip/Q-learning formalizes — a reviewer could say we are re-deriving Learn-to-Ask with Robins-style notation. Our defensible edge: they never state an estimand, never handle time-varying confounding by the history (they implicitly assume the expert's logged behavior is the thing to imitate, i.e. behavior-cloning-with-reward rather than counterfactual contrast), and they give no inference (no CIs on the blip, no value of the learned regime). Also they optimize the ASSISTANT's asking, not the user-side prompt. Must cite.

title: Learning Steerable Clarification Policies with Collaborative Self-play
venue_date: COLM 2026 (arXiv v1 3 Dec 2025, v3 13 Sep 2026). Authors: Jonathan Berant, Maximillian Chen, Adam Fisch, Reza Aghajani, Fantine Huot, Mirella Lapata, Jacob Eisenstein (Google DeepMind)
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Trains an assistant to choose among three actions on an ambiguous query: guess the intent and answer directly, enumerate several candidate intents, or ask a clarifying question. Training data comes from collaborative self-play between a user-simulator agent and the assistant. Crucially, the numeric COST of a clarification question and of each generated word is given to the model as input, and it is trained (via ReST / reinforced self-training) to maximize cost-penalized accuracy; it generalizes to unseen cost values at test time ('steerable').
overlap_with_us: This is the cleanest published instantiation of our STOP action: a learned, cost-penalized decision of whether to continue interacting or terminate and answer, with the cost exposed as a conditioning variable. It also uses a user simulator to generate the interaction distribution, which is the same device we would use for estimation. Differences: assistant-side rather than user-side treatment; the decision is a discrete 3-way action, not a language-valued treatment; no causal identification, no time-varying confounder formalism, no blip/Q estimation, no offline logged-data setting. We should frame our STOP contribution as 'optimal stopping inside an identified sequential regime with inference', not as 'first to have a stop action'.

title: Implicit Turn-Wise Policy Optimization for Proactive User-LLM Interaction (ITPO)
venue_date: arXiv:2603.23550 [cs.LG], submitted 21 Mar 2026. Authors: Haoyu Wang, Yuxin Chen, Liang Luo, Buyun Zhang, Ellie Dingqiao Wen, Pan Li
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Targets multi-turn human-AI collaboration where the only reward is a sparse terminal outcome and the user's replies are stochastic. It fits an IMPLICIT PROCESS REWARD MODEL that derives fine-grained, TURN-WISE process rewards from the sparse outcome signal, arguing turn-level signals are far more robust than token-level ones and that a turn is the natural atomic unit of credit. Plugs into PPO/GRPO/RLOO; evaluated on math tutoring, document writing and medical recommendation. Explicitly no causal or confounding discussion.
overlap_with_us: Their per-turn decomposition of a terminal reward is the machine-learning analogue of our blip function: 'how much did turn t contribute to final quality, holding history fixed'. The application domains (tutoring, document writing) are ours. Threat is that a reviewer reads our blip/Q estimation as 'ITPO with extra notation'. Our separation: they estimate a reward-shaping heuristic with no identification argument and no handling of the fact that the history is a time-varying confounder affected by prior treatment (the exact reason naive per-turn regression is biased); they have no STOP action and no target of inference. Strong citation for 'turn as the unit of credit assignment'.

title: CollabLLM: From Passive Responders to Active Collaborators
venue_date: ICML 2025, Outstanding Paper Award (arXiv v1 2 Feb 2025, revisions to 29 Jul 2025). Authors: Shirley Wu, Michel Galley, Baolin Peng, Hao Cheng, Gavin Li, Yao Dou, Weixin Cai, James Zou, Jure Leskovec, Jianfeng Gao
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Argues LLMs are trained myopically on the immediate next turn, and instead introduces 'Multiturn-aware Rewards': for a candidate response, it runs a COLLABORATIVE SIMULATION forward with a simulated user and scores the response by its long-term contribution to task completion and user satisfaction, then does reinforcement fine-tuning on that reward. Trained models actively uncover user intent and volunteer suggestions. Human study with 201 judges: +18.5% task performance, +46.3% interactivity, +17.6% satisfaction, -10.4% conversation time.
overlap_with_us: The multiturn-aware reward is literally a Monte-Carlo rollout estimate of a Q-function for a language-valued action under a simulated user — i.e. our Q/blip target, estimated by forward simulation instead of by identification from observed data. It is a high-visibility ICML Outstanding Paper, so reviewers will know it and will ask what causal identification buys over 'just roll out the simulator'. Our answer must be crisp: they need an accurate generative user model and on-policy access; we want estimands identified from OBSERVED logged human conversations under sequential ignorability, with inference and a stopping rule, and we intervene on the user side. Non-negotiable citation.

title: RL with Learnable Textual Feedback: A Bilevel Approach (Bi-NAC)
venue_date: arXiv:2605.24547 [cs.LG], submitted 23 May 2026. Authors: Utsav Singh, Sidhaarth Sredharan, Souradip Chakraborty, Amrit Singh Bedi
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Bilevel Natural Language Actor-Critic jointly trains an actor LLM and a critic LLM that GENERATES NATURAL-LANGUAGE FEEDBACK consumed in the actor's context. The stated insight is that feedback should not merely be correct but must actually improve the actor's policy — fluent, locally-correct critiques often fail to help. They formalize the coupling as a Stackelberg bilevel program and optimize the two end-to-end. No causal-inference framing; 'intervention' is my characterization, not theirs.
overlap_with_us: This is the closest published version of our component (iii): a generative language policy trained against a critic, where the criterion for the text is its downstream effect on another model's output. It also anticipates our key argument ('feedback must be causally effective, not just correct'). What is missing and is ours to claim: the critic is a learned scalar/text bilevel objective, not an identified causal blip/Q-function; there is no time-varying confounding by dialogue history, no multi-turn regime with stopping, and no estimation/inference guarantees. Our pitch should be 'the critic is a causal critic'.

title: Towards Better Agents for Multi-Turn User Interaction: The Next User Turn Is More Than Context (FACA)
venue_date: arXiv:2608.17499 [cs.AI], submitted 18 Aug 2026. Authors: Yiwen Zhao, Zhihao Wen, Yuchen Mao, Mingxuan Jiang, Yihao Hu, Pan Wang, Xin Zhang, Wei Wu
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Claims the next user turn is 'noisy, temporally local evidence about the preceding segment', not just context. Feedback-Aware Credit Assignment aligns each user reaction with the agent segment that preceded it, derives a locally normalized reaction advantage, and adds it to the verified terminal-outcome advantage — no extra critic, no extra rollouts. Reports +5.91 and +10.22 points nine-domain average over an outcome-only Interactive GRPO control at 8B and 14B across three seeds, and a placebo-style check (randomizing reaction polarity removes the Telecom gain).
overlap_with_us: Uses the user's next message as the measurement of the effect of the preceding turn — the same signal we treat as treatment/outcome-relevant, and their polarity-randomization check is a crude placebo test of exactly the causal claim we would make properly. Overlaps our (i) at the level of 'per-turn credit from local user feedback'. It is heuristic advantage shaping with no estimand, no confounding-by-history handling, no STOP action, and the user side is not being optimized. Useful as evidence that the field is groping toward our blip function without the causal apparatus.

title: Aligning Language Models from User Interactions
venue_date: arXiv:2603.12273 [cs.CL], submitted 18 Feb 2026. Authors: Thomas Kleine Buening, Jonas Hübotter, Barna Pásztor, Idan Shenfeld, Giorgia Ramponi, Andreas Krause (ETH Zurich / MIT)
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Learns from naturally occurring multi-turn interactions with no explicit feedback labels: a user follow-up message is read as evidence that the previous response was wrong, failed an instruction, or missed a preference. They condition the model on the follow-up, look at how the token distribution shifts, and self-distill that 'hindsight' distribution back into the model. Demonstrated for alignment on WildChat, personalization to individual users, and continual learning from deployment traffic. No causal or confounding discussion.
overlap_with_us: Same raw object as our project — the user's next prompt in a real logged conversation — and the same insight that it carries information about the quality of what came before. But they use the user turn as a free supervision signal for the ASSISTANT, whereas we treat it as the time-varying TREATMENT whose sequential effect we identify and then optimize. Their hindsight-conditioning is uncontrolled for history (a follow-up is generated after, and is confounded by, everything earlier), which is precisely the gap our g-formula/blip framing fills. Strong related work; a credible group, so cite carefully rather than ignore.

title: Training Proactive and Personalized LLM Agents (UserVille + PPP)
venue_date: COLM 2026 (arXiv v1 4 Nov 2025, revised 23 Aug 2026). Authors: Weiwei Sun, Xuhui Zhou, Weihua Du, Xingyao Wang, Sean Welleck, Graham Neubig, Maarten Sap, Yiming Yang (CMU)
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Builds UserVille, an interactive environment with LLM user simulators carrying diverse, configurable user preferences, and PPP, a multi-objective RL method optimizing Productivity, Proactivity and Personalization jointly. Rewards combine task completion, a 'question effort' penalty, and preference adherence, so the agent learns when asking the user is worth the interruption. Trained agents ask fewer but more targeted questions while beating baselines.
overlap_with_us: Occupies the 'cost of interacting with the user' half of our STOP action, and the configurable-preference simulator is a plausible testbed for our estimation. Assistant-side, simulator-only, purely optimization: no estimand, no identification from logged human data, no inference on the regime's value. Cite as the benchmark/environment precedent for interaction-cost-aware regimes.

title: How to Train Your Advisor: Steering Black-Box LLMs with Advisor Models
venue_date: ICML 2026 (arXiv v1 2 Oct 2025, v3 15 May 2026). Authors: Parth Asawa, Alan Zhu, Abigail O'Neill, Matei Zaharia, Alexandros G. Dimakis, Joseph E. Gonzalez (UC Berkeley)
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Trains a small open-weight 'Advisor' model to emit dynamic, PER-INSTANCE natural-language advice that is injected to steer a frozen black-box frontier model (GPT/Gemini class), since the frontier weights cannot be touched. Reports +27.4% on a tax-related task with GPT-5.2, -24.6% steps on a software-engineering agent task, transfer of advisors between student and frontier models, and no degradation on untested benchmarks. The abstract page presents it as per-instance/single-shot advice rather than multi-turn; training method details are not in the abstract, so 'RL-trained' is not something I can assert from the abstract alone.
overlap_with_us: A high-profile ICML 2026 precedent for 'learn a language-valued policy whose action is text sent to another model, optimized for that model's output quality' — i.e. our (iii) minus the sequential and causal parts. The gap we exploit: single-turn/per-instance, no conversation history as confounder, no sequential effects, no stopping decision, no identification. This is the paper to cite when we say the community already accepts 'language as a learned action'.

title: Prompting Policies for Multi-step Reasoning and Tool-Use in Black-box LLMs with Iterative Distillation of Experience
venue_date: arXiv:2605.14443 [cs.AI], submitted 14 May 2026. Authors: Krishna Sayana, Ketan Todi, Ambarish Jash
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] A lightweight 'prompter' model is optimized to maximize task-specific reward for a larger frozen worker LLM on multi-step reasoning and tool-use tasks. The distinctive mechanism is a contrastive experience buffer that pairs scalar rewards with dense TEXTUAL critiques, which lets them amortize what would be iterative prompt refinement into single-shot policy weights. Whether it operates over genuine multi-turn exchanges is not established by the abstract.
overlap_with_us: Uses our exact phrase 'prompting policies' and learns a policy over prompts for a frozen model, so it is a naming/terminology collision we should be aware of. Substantively weaker than Prompt-R1 for our purposes: amortizes refinement into a single shot (explicitly collapsing the sequential structure we want to keep), no stop action, no causal estimand. Cite in the prompt-policy paragraph.

title: Prompt Optimization with Logged Bandit Data
venue_date: arXiv:2504.02646 [cs.LG], submitted 3 Apr 2025. Authors: Haruka Kiyohara, Daniel Yiming Cao, Yuta Saito, Thorsten Joachims (Cornell)
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Off-policy learning for prompt selection from naturally logged user feedback (clicks) in an LLM pipeline generating personalized sentences. They show naive off-policy gradient estimation is problematic in this setting and propose a kernel-based estimator that exploits similarity among generated sentences to cut variance while controlling bias. Evaluated on a new benchmark for personalized movie-recommendation descriptions, with gains largest when the prompt candidate set is big. Explicitly a SINGLE-STAGE CONTEXTUAL BANDIT setting, not sequential or multi-turn.
overlap_with_us: The methodological precedent closest to our estimation machinery: prompts treated as actions, logged feedback, off-policy estimation with explicit bias-variance control, by an OPE group (Saito/Joachims). This is the paper a methods reviewer will name when asking 'what is new beyond off-policy prompt optimization?'. Our answer is exactly the dimension they disclaim: one stage vs. sequential, no time-varying confounder, no blip/g-computation, no stopping rule. Cite prominently as the single-stage special case we generalize.

title: Offline RL by Reward-Weighted Fine-Tuning for Conversation Optimization
venue_date: NeurIPS 2025 (Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38); arXiv v1 8 Jun 2025, v3 16 Feb 2026. Authors: Subhojyoti Mukherjee, Viet Dac Lai, Raghavendra Addanki, Ryan Rossi, Seunghyun Yoon, Trung Bui, Anup Rao, Jayakumar Subramanian, Branislav Kveton (Adobe)
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Recasts offline RL with LLMs as reward-weighted fine-tuning solvable with standard SFT machinery — training on trajectories weighted by realized reward rather than using importance weighting. The target is short-horizon, FIXED-LENGTH question-answering policies where the agent either reasons about candidate answers or asks clarifying questions. Claims gains in both optimized reward and language quality over SFT/DPO baselines.
overlap_with_us: Offline, logged-data policy learning for multi-turn conversation, which is our data setting, and it deliberately avoids importance weighting — so it is the 'no-causal-machinery' offline alternative a reviewer may prefer for its simplicity. Our differentiators: fixed horizon (they assume it, we want an endogenous STOP), no time-varying confounding correction (reward weighting is not identification), user-side treatment, and inference. Cite in the offline-RL-vs-DTR comparison.

title: Eliciting Behaviors in Multi-Turn Conversations
venue_date: arXiv:2512.23701 [cs.CL], submitted 29 Dec 2025. Authors: Jing Huang, Shujian Zhang, Lun Wang, Andrew Hard, Rajiv Mathews, John Lambert (Google)
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Extends behavior elicitation (finding natural-language prompts that induce a target behavior) from single-turn to multi-turn. They taxonomize methods into three families by how they interact with the target model — prior knowledge only, offline interactions, and learning from ONLINE interactions — and give a generalized multi-turn formulation of the online method that unifies single- and multi-turn elicitation. They then study the query-budget vs. success-rate tradeoff: online methods hit 45/19/77% success across three tasks with a few thousand target-model queries, where static multi-turn benchmarks find few or no failures.
overlap_with_us: Their online multi-turn method IS a learned policy that maps conversation context to the next user-side turn in order to move the target model's output — structurally identical to our prompt policy, but with an adversarial objective (elicit a bad behavior) instead of task quality, and with a query budget rather than a STOP action. Nothing causal. Best used as evidence that 'learn the next user turn against a frozen model' is an established, working primitive, and as a possible second evaluation domain.

title: IntentRL: Training Proactive User-intent Agents for Open-ended Deep Research via Reinforcement Learning
venue_date: arXiv:2602.03468 [cs.AI, cs.LG], submitted 3 Feb 2026. Authors: Haohao Luo, Zexi Li, Yuexiang Xie, Wenhao Zhang, Yaliang Li, Ying Shen
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Deep-research agents waste large compute on vague queries, so IntentRL trains them to clarify BEFORE launching expensive research. A data pipeline expands seed examples into dialogues via a 'shallow-to-deep intent refinement graph'; then two-stage RL: Stage I on offline dialogues to learn general interaction patterns, Stage II live against a user simulator (hybrid rule-based + LLM-judge rewards) to sharpen responsiveness to varied feedback. Reports better clarification accuracy and better final research quality than comparable commercial clarification features.
overlap_with_us: Offline-then-simulator two-stage recipe over multi-turn clarification, with an implicit cost-of-research motivation for asking vs. proceeding. Assistant-side, no causal identification, no formal stopping rule, no estimand. Mainly relevant as a recent applied instance of 'learned interaction policy' and as a source of the offline-to-online training pattern we might mirror.

title: No More Stale Feedback: Co-Evolving Critics for Open-World Agent Learning (ECHO)
venue_date: arXiv:2601.06794 [cs.AI], v1 11 Jan 2026, v2 14 Apr 2026. Authors: Zhicong Li, Lingjie Jiang, Yulan Hu, Xingchen Zeng, Yixia Li, Xiangwen Zhang, Guanhua Chen, Zheng Pan, Xin Li, Yong Liu
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Observes that in critique-guided RL the agent's error distribution drifts as it improves, so a static critic goes stale. ECHO (Evolving Critic for Hindsight-guided Optimization) co-evolves policy and critic in a synchronized loop, with a cascaded rollout where the critic produces several diagnoses before policy refinement, saturation-aware gain shaping to avoid plateaus on already-strong trajectories, and dual-track GRPO updates to keep feedback aligned with the current policy. Reports more stable training and higher long-horizon success in open-world tasks.
overlap_with_us: Relevant to (iii) as the 'critic must track the policy' problem we will hit when training a generative prompt policy against a fitted causal critic — and it names the failure mode (stale critic under policy drift) that in our language is the critic being fit under the wrong behavior distribution. No causal identification, no user-side treatment, no stopping. Cite as a practical precedent for co-training schedules.

title: Hey Chat, Can You Teach Me? Structuring Socratic Dialogue for Human Learning in the Wild
venue_date: arXiv:2606.11744 [cs.CL], submitted 10 Jun 2026, 10 pages + appendices. Authors: Sidney Tio, Arunesh Sinha, Pradeep Varakantham
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Builds a prerequisite knowledge graph over subtopics, then frames tutoring as a sequential decision problem: a lightweight PPO policy chooses WHICH NODE to teach next AND HOW MANY DIALOGUE TURNS to spend before moving on, while an LLM conducts the actual Socratic exchange at that node and returns a student-progress signal. Reported to beat scaling-only baselines on held-out STEM and non-STEM topics. The abstract does not spell out the full action space.
overlap_with_us: One of the few papers with an explicit learned decision about WHEN TO STOP the current line of interaction and move on — the closest thing to our STOP action in a tutoring application, and it cleanly separates a small decision policy from the LLM that renders the utterance (a factorization we may want, since it makes the treatment low-dimensional). But the action is a discrete curriculum choice, not language-valued; and there is no causal identification, no confounding by history, no outcome-quality estimand. Cite for the 'small policy + LLM renderer' design and for turn-budget decisions.

title: Whom to Query for What: Adaptive Group Elicitation via Multi-Turn LLM Interactions
venue_date: ICML 2026 (arXiv v1 15 Feb 2026, revised 2 Jun 2026). Authors: Ruomeng Ding, Tianwei Gao, Thomas P. Zollo, Eitan Bachmat, Richard Zemel, Zhun Deng
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Formalizes adaptive group elicitation: over multiple rounds, an agent picks both WHICH QUESTION to ask and WHICH RESPONDENT to ask, under explicit query and participation budgets. Candidate questions are scored by LLM-based expected-information-gain objectives; a heterogeneous GNN aggregates responses and respondent attributes to impute missing answers and guide who to query next. Improves population-level response prediction on three opinion datasets, e.g. >12% relative gain on CES at a 10% respondent budget. Described as theoretically grounded but the abstract shows no causal framework.
overlap_with_us: An ICML 2026 paper on sequential, budget-constrained adaptive elicitation via multi-turn LLM interaction — same decision-theoretic shape as our adaptive regime, but the objective is information gain about a population, not task quality, and the treatment is a selection from a candidate set, not generated language. No causal estimand. Modest overlap; cite for adaptive-elicitation-under-budget.

title: Asking Clarifying Questions for Preference Elicitation With Large Language Models
venue_date: arXiv:2510.12015 [cs.AI], submitted 13 Oct 2025. Authors: Ali Montazeralghaem, Guy Tennenholtz, Craig Boutilier, Ofer Meshi (Google)
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Trains an LLM to ask a SEQUENCE of clarifying questions that reveal a user's preferences, using a diffusion-inspired two-stage scheme: a forward process takes a full user profile, generates clarifying questions, and progressively deletes answers to 'noise' the profile; the reverse process trains the model to 'denoise' the profile by asking effective questions. Targets conversational recommendation with sparse user history, claimed to be domain-agnostic. The abstract specifies no stopping criterion.
overlap_with_us: Sequential question-asking policy for eliciting latent user information — same authors as Controllable User Simulation, so this Google group is circling the whole space we are in. Relevant to (ii) but the objective is profile recovery, the training signal is synthetic noising rather than outcome quality, and there is no causal identification or stopping rule. Adjacent; cite alongside the other elicitation work.

title: Causal methods for LLM development and evaluation
venue_date: KDD 2026 (arXiv v1 25 May 2026). Authors: Dennis Frauen, Marie Brockschmidt, Konstantin Hess, Haorui Ma, Yuchen Ma, Abdurahman Maarouf, Maresa Schröder, Jonas Schweisthal, Yuxin Wang, Athiya Deviyani, Sonali Parbhoo, Rahul G. Krishnan, Stefan Feuerriegel
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] A survey/position paper (Feuerriegel's LMU group plus Parbhoo and Krishnan) arguing causal methods are underutilized across the LLM pipeline. It explains how causal methods handle confounding and distribution shift in logged data, maps opportunities across pretraining, alignment, routing, agentic workflows and evaluation, and lists research directions. Interventions are treated generically ('what is the effect of adding a data domain during pretraining?'); per the abstract it does NOT develop prompts or agent actions as time-varying treatments, nor dynamic treatment regimes, nor sequential OPE machinery.
overlap_with_us: Positioning gold rather than a threat: a KDD 2026 survey by credible causal-ML people that explicitly flags sequential/agentic LLM interaction as an open opportunity for causal methods without doing it. Cite it in our intro as the community's own statement of the gap we fill. Caveat: a search snippet paraphrased it as already covering sequential identifiability and OPE for agentic systems — that framing is OVERSTATED relative to the abstract, so we should read the full paper before leaning on it, in case a body section stakes a closer claim.

title: LLM-as-a-Tutor: Policy-Aware Prompt Adaptation for Non-Verifiable RL
venue_date: arXiv:2607.04412 [cs.AI], v1 5 Jul 2026, v2 9 Aug 2026. Authors: Yujin Kim, Namgyu Ho, Sangmin Hwang, Joonkee Kim, Yongjin Yang, Sangmin Bae, Seungone Kim, Jaehun Jung, Se-Young Yun, Hwanjun Song
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Notes that in RL for non-verifiable tasks the TRAINING PROMPTS stay static, drawn from fixed corpora. An LLM acts as both examiner and generator: it detects prompts that no longer produce meaningful performance variation across the policy's outputs, then appends atomic constraints to them, escalating difficulty as the policy improves. This yields a self-calibrating training signal without an external difficulty schedule.
overlap_with_us: Only structurally related: a model generating prompts adapted to another model's current state, i.e. language as an adaptive intervention. But the goal is curriculum difficulty for training, not task quality at interaction time; no multi-turn regime, no stopping, no causal estimand. Background — cite at most in passing under 'adaptive prompt generation'.

title: What to Edit Next: Visually Aligned Image-Editing Follow-Up Suggestions in Conversational Systems
venue_date: arXiv:2608.07565 [cs.CV], v1 3 Aug 2026, revised 18 Aug 2026. Authors: Zhijing Zhang, Jinpeng Yu, Xin Song, Bingnan Li, Chuyue Li, Changhui Du, Xiaolin Fang, Jiaming Liu, Ruihua Huang (Qwen App)
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] A deployed system that proposes the USER'S NEXT PROMPT (follow-up image edit) in a conversational image-editing product, noting 80.1% of useful suggestions are image-dependent. Three stages: SFT on 100k real conversations with human-reviewed intents; multi-objective RL optimized against USER CLICK FEEDBACK to align suggestions with what users actually choose; then a visual verifier to cut inconsistency between the suggested edit and the current image. A large-scale randomized A/B test reports visual inconsistency 3.7%->0.9%, suggestion CTR +32.70%, image take-away rate +16.32%, turns per user +39.90% (p<0.05).
overlap_with_us: The strongest APPLICATION precedent for our exact framing — a learned policy over the user's next prompt, conditioned on the conversation/artifact state, trained from logged human interaction and validated by a randomized experiment. Use it as motivation and as proof that user-side prompt policies matter in production and can be A/B tested (relevant to our identification story: they got randomization, we are arguing from observational logs). It is engineering, not causal inference: clicks not task quality, no estimand, no confounding argument, no stopping rule.

title: Policy Iteration with Human Feedback: Bringing Post-Training RL to In-context Learning (PIHF)
venue_date: arXiv:2608.16831 [cs.AI, cs.CL], submitted 17 Aug 2026. Authors: Minh-Ha Nguyen, Cathy Shyr
what_it_does: [CONFIRMED — id and title match] Implements generalized policy iteration in natural language with frozen weights: an LLM critic plus a clinical expert inspect reasoning and tool trajectories, identify failure patterns, and propose revisions to a VERSIONED natural-language policy and toolset, with the expert holding accept/rollback authority; Recall@1/@5 validate each iteration. Reports +31.1 to +32.7 points on ultra-rare-disease diagnosis across multiple executors, arguing pretrained LLMs can serve as fixed-weight execution substrates for expert-guided policy refinement instead of retraining.
overlap_with_us: Only loosely related to (iii): treats human/critic feedback as a policy-improvement operator on a natural-language policy object, which is a nice framing to borrow, but the 'policy' is a prompt document revised offline by a human-in-the-loop, not a learned regime over turns. No causal identification, no time-varying confounding, no stopping. Background at most.

title: UNVERIFIED classics I did not individually confirm: TEMPERA (test-time prompt editing as an MDP) and PRewrite (prompt rewriting with RL)
venue_date: TEMPERA appears as ICLR 2023 in a University of Alberta course PDF; PRewrite arXiv v4. I did NOT fetch either abs page (web-search budget exhausted), so treat both ids/venues as UNCLEAR.
what_it_does: [UNCLEAR — not individually verified] Per secondary sources: TEMPERA casts test-time prompt editing as an MDP where the state is the current prompt plus query and the RL agent picks an editing operation from a designed action space, reporting ~5.33x sample-efficiency gains over few-shot fine-tuning; note one source rendered the title as 'Test-Time Prompting via Reinforcement Learning' rather than 'Test-Time Prompt Editing via Reinforcement Learning', so the exact title needs checking. Per secondary sources, PRewrite trains a rewriter LLM with RL to turn an under-optimized prompt into a better one, with the vocabulary as action space, decoded-tokens-so-far as state, and the task LLM's downstream performance as reward. Someone should re-verify both ids before they go in the bibliography.
overlap_with_us: These are the canonical 'prompt-as-MDP / prompt-policy' citations a reviewer will expect in our related work, and they establish that sequential prompt editing under RL is old news — which sharpens the requirement that our contribution be the causal identification, the STOP action and the inference, not the mere fact of a learned prompt policy.

title: Policy Learning with a Natural Language Action Space: A Causal Approach
venue_date: arXiv v1 2025-02-24, cs.CL; no conference venue listed on the abs page (v1 only)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (id and title match; authors Bohan Zhang, Yixin Wang, Paramveer Dhillon). Sets up multi-stage decision-making where the ACTIONS ARE NATURAL LANGUAGE and the outcome is only observed after the whole sequence, then estimates Dynamic Treatment Regimes by Q-learning with a single model instead of PPO's policy/value/reward triple. Optimization is gradient ascent on language embeddings, and their key technical piece is a decoding strategy that maps the optimized embedding back into coherent natural language. Evaluated on mental-health intervention, hate-speech countering, and sentiment transfer with human eval on transfer strength, content preservation, fluency.
overlap_with_us: Covers our (ii) almost exactly (optimal adaptive regime over language-valued actions via Q-learning/DTR) and pre-empts the core of (iii) (generate text by optimizing against the learned Q/critic, then decode). Does NOT have: a STOP/terminate action, user-side prompts in a human-LLM loop as the treatment, blip/SNMM decomposition, or any formal identification argument with conversation history as a time-varying confounder.

title: What is the Causal Effect of a Conversation? Estimands and Inference in AI Mediated Conversations
venue_date: arXiv v1 2026-07-03, stat.ME (Adriane Fresh, Aiden Shin)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED. Builds a potential-outcomes framework for causal inference when the treatment is a conversation, aimed at AI-mediated (generative-AI interlocutor) experiments. Its central point is that the conversation is generated JOINTLY by respondent and agent and is therefore endogenous, so randomizing assignment does not identify message-level or feature-level effects. It separates and gives distinct identifying assumptions for: assignment to a conversational condition, assignment to a conversational POLICY, the opening message, messages within a conversation, realized conversational features, and the full realized conversation, noting that some require sequential assumptions, representations of conversational histories, or explicit message-level interventions.
overlap_with_us: Directly occupies our (i) identification layer: turn-level language interventions, sequential/ignorability assumptions, and history representation as the confounder. It also already names 'assignment to a conversational policy' as an estimand, which is the object our (ii) optimizes. It is a framework/estimand paper only: no estimator, no blip/Q decomposition, no DML/g-estimation, no policy learning, no STOP action, no experiments.

title: Causal Inference with Video Features as Treatments
venue_date: arXiv v1 2026-07-07, v2 2026-09-15, stat.AP (Kentaro Nakamura, Adam Breuer, Michael Crespin, Bryce Dietrich, Kosuke Imai)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED. This is the sequential/longitudinal extension of the Imai-Nakamura 'generative-representation as treatment' program, applied to video rather than text. They regenerate each video with a deep generative model, use the model's internal representations as low-dimensional summaries of the high-dimensional treatment, prove nonparametric identification of the average potential-outcome TRAJECTORY under DYNAMIC STOCHASTIC INTERVENTIONS, and give a consistent, asymptotically normal estimator built on a longitudinal neural network. They also build a ground-truth benchmark (10,000 Super Mario Bros. levels played by fixed Mario AI agents) and apply it to 2020 U.S. presidential TV ads.
overlap_with_us: This is the single most dangerous method-transfer scoop for our (i): it is exactly 'high-dimensional generative-model-represented treatment, unfolding over time, latent dynamic confounding, identification of dynamic-intervention trajectories, longitudinal neural estimator' — with the modality swapped. Our differentiators must be: text/prompt treatment inside a closed human-LLM feedback loop (their agents are fixed, ours responds), blip/Q decomposition rather than trajectory means, optimal regime learning, and a STOP action. If we claim 'first sequential causal framework for high-dimensional generative treatments', this kills it.

title: Causal Inference for Human-Language Model Collaboration (CausalCollab)
venue_date: arXiv v1 2024-03-30; published NAACL 2024 Main Conference, pp. 1630-1647, Mexico City (Bohan Zhang, Yixin Wang, Paramveer Dhillon)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (arXiv id, title, and ACL Anthology entry all match). Studies human-LM collaboration where the LM proposes text and the human edits/responds, and asks the counterfactual 'what if the human had used a different editing/refinement strategy'. Because ATE is inapplicable to high-dimensional text treatments, they define a new estimand, the Incremental Stylistic Effect (ISE), the average effect of infinitesimally shifting a text toward a style (e.g. more formal), and establish nonparametric identification conditions. CausalCollab estimates ISE of interaction strategies in DYNAMIC human-LM collaboration across three scenarios, reducing confounding versus baselines.
overlap_with_us: Same substantive setting as us (human-side text is the treatment, human-LM interaction, dynamic history confounding) and same authors as the natural-language-action-space DTR paper, so this group is one paper away from our whole agenda. Covers part of (i). Differs in estimand: a directional derivative along one style axis, not a blip/Q function over arbitrary language interventions; no regime learning, no STOP, and the outcome is collaboration quality rather than a final task-quality outcome at a chosen stopping time.

title: DeepBlip: Estimating Conditional Average Treatment Effects Over Time
venue_date: arXiv v1 2025-11-18, stat.ML/cs.LG/stat.ME, 42 pages; no venue listed (Haorui Ma, Dennis Frauen, Stefan Feuerriegel)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED. First neural framework for Structural Nested Mean Models, which decompose the joint effect of a treatment sequence into localized time-specific BLIP EFFECTS. Their contribution is a 'double optimization trick' that lets all blip functions be learned simultaneously end-to-end, getting around the inherently sequential g-estimation recursion that blocks gradient-based training. Uses LSTMs/transformers for temporal dependencies, adjusts for time-varying confounding, and has a Neyman-orthogonal loss for robustness to nuisance misspecification; evaluated on clinical datasets.
overlap_with_us: This is precisely the estimation machinery our (i) needs, already built — including the explicit claim that blip decomposition 'enables the efficient offline evaluation of optimal treatment policies without re-computation', which is our (ii)'s justification. Treatments are low-dimensional/clinical, not language-valued, and there is no text, no LLM, no generative policy. Realistically this is our baseline and our citation-of-record, and 'first neural SNMM' is already taken.

title: Causal Inference with Generative Artificial Intelligence: Application to Texts as Treatments (GPI)
venue_date: arXiv v1 2024-10-01, latest v5 2026-06-11, stat.AP/cs.CL/cs.LG; a JASA-formatted manuscript is posted on Imai's site (Kosuke Imai, Kentaro Nakamura)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED, with one caveat worth flagging: the SAME arXiv id has circulated under two titles across versions ('Causal Inference with Generative Artificial Intelligence...' on the current abs page vs 'Causal REPRESENTATION LEARNING with Generative Artificial Intelligence...' on v1/v4 HTML), so a citation using either title is legitimate and is not a mismatch. They use an LLM to GENERATE the treatment texts and then use the LLM's true internal representation for estimation, which disentangles the target treatment feature (sentiment, topic) from unknown confounding features and removes the need to learn causal representation from data. They establish nonparametric identification of the ATE, give an estimation strategy that avoids overlap violations, derive asymptotics via double machine learning, extend to human-perception-based treatment features with instrumental variables, and cover text reuse; simulations plus empirical study with Llama 3.
overlap_with_us: Covers the single-shot version of our (i): identification and DML estimation for a text-valued treatment using generative-model representations. Not sequential, no history-as-time-varying-confounder, no blip/Q, no policy. But note this is the parent of arXiv:2607.06126 above, so the sequential text version is the obvious next paper from that group.

title: Optimizing Prompts for Large Language Models: A Causal Approach (CPO)
venue_date: arXiv 2026-02-02, cs.AI/cs.LG (Wei Chen, Yanbin Fang, Shuran Fu, Fasheng Xu, Xuan Wei)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED. Reframes automatic prompt optimization as causal estimation: stage one learns an OFFLINE CAUSAL REWARD MODEL by applying Double Machine Learning to semantic embeddings of prompts and queries, explicitly isolating the causal effect of prompt variation from confounding query attributes; stage two uses that debiased reward to guide a cheap search for query-specific prompts without online evaluation. Their stated motivation is that existing dynamic APO methods rely on reward models that are 'fundamentally correlational, confounding prompt effectiveness with query characteristics'. Beats human prompts and SOTA optimizers on math reasoning, visualization, and data analytics, with gains concentrated on hard queries.
overlap_with_us: This is our (iii) in single-turn form, and it has already published the framing 'existing prompt reward models are correlational, ours is causal' — the exact rhetorical position we planned to take with the causal critic. It is single-turn (prompt, query) with no sequence, no time-varying confounding, no blip/Q, no STOP, and it does search rather than training a generative policy. We must cite it and differentiate on sequentiality.

title: Causal Risk Minimization for High-Dimensional Treatments
venue_date: arXiv 2026-05-26, cs.LG/stat.ML, 18 pages, 4 figures; no venue listed (Nikita Dhawan, Arnav Paruthi, Andrew Kim, Lovedeep Gondara, Jekaterina Novikova, Chris J. Maddison)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED. Recasts causal inference as a learning problem for treatment spaces so large that classical estimators' assumption of observing all interventions fails — explicitly naming 'the space of all text strings'. Under no-unobserved-confounding they show causal error decomposes into a series of MOMENT-BALANCING ERRORS OF INCREASING ORDER and build objectives that optimize those directly. They also project the effect of a high-dimensional treatment onto lower-dimensional treatment ATTRIBUTES so one model answers many causal questions without attribute-specific retraining; experiments on high-dimensional continuous, discrete, and text treatments (semi-synthetic Amazon Reviews).
overlap_with_us: Occupies the estimation-theory slot for our (i) when the treatment is language: higher-order balance objectives plus attribute projection is a credible alternative to our blip/Q route, and the attribute-projection trick is the clean answer to 'which feature of the prompt mattered'. Single-stage only, no sequence, no policy learning, no STOP.

title: Natural Language Actor-Critic: Scalable Off-Policy Learning in Language Space (NLAC)
venue_date: arXiv v1 2025-12-04, v2 2026-02-02, cs.LG/cs.CL; no venue listed (Joey Hong, Kang Liu, Zhan Ling, Jiecao Chen, Sergey Levine)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED. Actor-critic algorithm for LLM agents in which the CRITIC IS A GENERATIVE LLM THAT OUTPUTS NATURAL LANGUAGE rather than a scalar value, and that language feedback is the training signal for the actor. This enables off-policy learning without policy gradients and targets long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks (tool use, web browsing, dialogue with people) by using natural-language explanations to direct policy improvement instead of random exploration.
overlap_with_us: Covers the architecture of our (iii) — train a generative language policy against a learned critic in a multi-turn, delayed-outcome setting — and does it at scale. Crucially it is pure RL: no identification, no confounding adjustment, no propensity/orthogonality, no treatment-effect estimand. Our defensible claim narrows to 'the critic is a CAUSALLY identified blip/Q function under time-varying confounding', not 'we train a policy against a critic'.

title: What if LLMs Ate Their Words: Causal History Effects in Multi-Turn Interaction
venue_date: arXiv 2026-09-05, 11 pages, 6 figures, code/data on GitHub (Jinnan Li, Zheren Fu, Yue Wang, Jinzhe Li, Yuan Wu, Yi Chang)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED. Empirically intervenes on CONVERSATION HISTORY in completed multi-turn trajectories: it replays the user messages actually observed while editing only the assistant-generated history, across six task families and five models. 'Neutralization' (replacing prior assistant responses with neutral content) shifts downstream min-max normalized performance by +.027 over 2,973 trajectories, and a length-matched control (+.069 vs +.068) rules out mere context shortening. 'Turn Surgery' intervenes on one assistant turn at a time: among 237 degraded trajectories, 63.7% contain at least one beneficial intervention and 48.4% of binary tasks admit a fail-to-success reversal.
overlap_with_us: Strongest available empirical evidence that conversation history is causally active, i.e. that our time-varying confounder/mediator story is real and that turn-level counterfactuals in language are estimable by replay. It intervenes on the ASSISTANT side, not the user prompt side, which is our treatment; and it is a measurement study with no estimand, no identification result, no policy, no STOP. Useful as motivation and as a possible semi-synthetic validation design rather than a competitor.

title: Structured Learning of Compositional Sequential Interventions
venue_date: arXiv v1 2024-06-09, v2 2024-10-29; camera-ready NeurIPS 2024 (Jialin Yu, Andreas Koukorinis, Nicolo Colombo, Yuchen Zhu, Ricardo Silva)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED. Considers sequential regimes where each unit receives COMBINATIONS of interventions over time and interventions are described by QUALITATIVE LABELS (their examples: 'close schools for a month due to a pandemic', 'promote this podcast to this user during this week'). They argue black-box sequence models rely on poorly understood generalization assumptions and degrade under sparse sequences, temporal variability, and LARGE ACTION SPACES, so they posit an explicit compositional model that isolates intervention effects into modules and prove identification of combined effects at different units and time steps, inspired by causal matrix factorization.
overlap_with_us: The closest existing answer to 'sequential + huge/linguistically-described action space + generalize to unseen intervention combinations', which is the generalization problem underneath our (i) and (ii). Interventions are discrete labels rather than free-form text, the target is prediction for novel compositions rather than effect estimation or policy learning, and there is no STOP action or generative policy.

title: Off-Policy Evaluation for Large Action Spaces via Embeddings (MIPS)
venue_date: arXiv 2022-02-13 (rev. 2022-06-16); ICML 2022 (Yuta Saito, Thorsten Joachims)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (ICML 2022; a companion ICML 2023 paper, proceedings.mlr.press/v202 saito23b, extends it via conjunct effect modeling, and arXiv:2305.03954 learns the embeddings instead of hand-specifying them). Shows IPS-based off-policy estimators collapse in bias and variance when the action count is large, explicitly citing language models as a foiled application, and replaces action-level importance weights with MARGINALIZED importance weights over an ACTION EMBEDDING. Characterizes bias, variance, and MSE and the conditions under which the embedding gives a statistical gain.
overlap_with_us: This is the off-the-shelf tool for the 'infinite action space' half of our (ii)/(iii): if we need off-policy value estimates for a prompting regime over language actions, marginalizing over prompt embeddings is the established answer and a reviewer will ask why we did not use or compare to it. Contextual-bandit single-step, not sequential, and no confounding-identification framing.

title: Adaptive Stopping for Multi-Turn LLM Reasoning (MiCP)
venue_date: arXiv v1 2026-04-01, last revised v3 2026-08-14, cs.CL/cs.AI (Xiaofan Zhou, Huy Nguyen, Bo Yu, Chenxi Liu, Lu Cheng)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED. Directly targets 'When should the model stop?' in multi-turn reasoning and interaction (adaptive RAG, ReAct-style agents), arguing existing work uses heuristic stopping rules or fixed turn budgets with no guarantee the final prediction still contains the right answer. Proposes MiCP, a multi-level conformal prediction framework that allocates different error budgets across turns so the pipeline can stop early while retaining an overall coverage guarantee.
overlap_with_us: The only paper I found that formalizes the STOP decision in multi-turn LLM interaction, so it is the incumbent our (ii) STOP action will be compared against. It is distribution-free/conformal, not causal: no treatment effects, no confounding, no optimal-regime learning, and stopping is about coverage of the answer set rather than about the value of continuing. A causal DTR with an explicit STOP action over prompt interventions still appears unclaimed.

title: Causal methods for LLM development and evaluation
venue_date: arXiv 2026-05-25; published at KDD 2026 (Frauen, Brockschmidt, Hess, Ma, Ma, Maarouf, Schroder, Schweisthal, Wang, Deviyani, Parbhoo, Krishnan, Feuerriegel)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED. Position/survey paper arguing that central questions in LLM development are inherently causal (effect of adding a pretraining data domain, annotator preference shifts under style changes, routing a prompt to a larger vs smaller model under cost constraints) and that causal methods are underrepresented despite logged data being confounded, judges being biased, and deployments being non-stationary. Maps opportunities across pretraining, alignment, routing, agentic workflows, and evaluation, and lists research openings — including off-policy evaluation with structured mediators, dynamic confounding across time, and limited support with costly end-to-end feedback.
overlap_with_us: Does not compete, but it publicly stakes out our research opening as an opening (dynamic confounding over time + costly end-to-end feedback in agentic workflows), and it shares authors with DeepBlip (Ma, Frauen, Feuerriegel). Treat as the agenda-setting citation, and as a signal that the DeepBlip group may be heading for the LLM-sequential version themselves.

title: The Confounder Trap: Treatment-Encoding Representations in Causal Inference with Text
venue_date: arXiv 2026-07-28, stat.ME/cs.CL/stat.AP/stat.ML (Marie Neubrander, Graham Tierney, Alexander Volfovsky)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED. Shows that when treatment status is itself encoded by words in the text, representations learned from the full text directly encode the treatment, so RICHER representations can INDUCE overlap/positivity violations even when the underlying causal problem satisfies overlap. Proposes masking the treatment-defining lexical signal before learning the representation: deletion masking preserves overlap for simpler models, replacement masking is the practical option for LLMs. Reports improved overlap diagnostics and reduced bias in effect estimates.
overlap_with_us: Not a competitor but a direct threat to our identification story: if we embed the user's prompt as the treatment and embed the conversation history as the confounder, the history embedding will encode the prompt and our sequential positivity/overlap at each turn collapses exactly as described. We should adopt or at least address masking, and a reviewer who knows this paper will ask.

title: Estimating Causal Effects of Text Interventions Leveraging LLMs (CausalDANN)
venue_date: arXiv v1 2024-10-28, v2 2025-03-20, v3 2026-03-14; published in Findings of IJCNLP 2025 (Siyi Guo, Myrl G. Marmarelis, Fred Morstatter, Kristina Lerman)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (arXiv abs page lists no venue, but ACL Anthology 2025.findings-ijcnlp.10 confirms publication, and an OpenReview record exists). Estimates effects of ARBITRARY textual interventions by having an LLM perform the text transformation (e.g. reducing anger in a social-media post) to construct the counterfactual treatment, since real interventions are infeasible and classical methods assume binary/discrete treatments. Adds a text-level classifier with domain-adaptation ability so effect estimates stay robust to the domain shift induced by the rewriting, and works even when only the control group is observed.
overlap_with_us: Gives the practical recipe for generating counterfactual language treatments with an LLM, which is how we will have to construct counterfactual user turns for our (i). Single-shot, social-media outcomes, no sequence, no history confounding, no policy learning; the LLM is the rewriter, not the environment being steered.

title: Causal Effect Inference for Structured Treatments (SIN)
venue_date: NeurIPS 2021 (proceedings.neurips.cc, paper d02e9bdc27a894e882fa0c9055c99722); arXiv:2106.01939 (Jean Kaddour, Yuchen Zhu, Qi Liu, Matt J. Kusner, Ricardo Silva)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (verified via the NeurIPS 2021 proceedings page and the arXiv listing; I did not open the abs page itself). Estimates CATEs when treatments are structured objects — the abstract names graphs, images, AND TEXTS — under the twin problems of missing interventions and confounding. The contribution is a generalized Robinson decomposition that isolates the causal estimand to reduce regularization bias, admits arbitrary plug-in learners, and carries a quasi-oracle convergence guarantee; experiments on small-world and molecular graphs.
overlap_with_us: The canonical prior art for 'treatment is a high-dimensional structured object', and its generalized Robinson/R-learner decomposition is the natural single-stage ancestor of a blip-style orthogonalized loss for language treatments. Static single-stage, graph experiments, no sequence and no policy.

title: Contrastive representations of high-dimensional, structured treatments
venue_date: arXiv 2024-11-28, stat.ML/cs.AI/cs.LG; no venue listed (Oriol Corcoll Andreu, Athanasios Vlontzos, Michael O'Riordan, Ciaran M. Gilligan-Lee)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED. Notes treatments in many real settings are structured high-dimensional objects such as text, video, or audio, and shows that exploiting shared structure across treatments BLINDLY (in order to generalize to unseen treatments at test time) leads to BIASED causal effect estimates. Devises a contrastive objective to learn a treatment representation, proves it identifies the underlying causal factors while discarding non-causally-relevant ones, and proves the resulting representation yields unbiased effect estimates; validated on synthetic and real data.
overlap_with_us: Relevant to the representation step of our (i): it is the formal warning that an off-the-shelf prompt embedding is not a valid treatment representation, plus a proposed fix. Static single-stage, no sequential extension, no policy learning; pairs with The Confounder Trap as the two representation-validity hazards we must address.

title: Structural Nested Mean Models for Modified Treatment Policies
venue_date: arXiv v1 2025-09-26, v2 2025-10-06, stat.ME (Zach Shahn)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED. Extends SNMMs to Modified Treatment Policy settings, i.e. interventions defined relative to the NATURAL treatment value a unit would have received absent intervention (more realistic than setting exposure to one ideal level for everyone). Works both under the Richardson-Robins (2013) SWIG exchangeability conditions and under parallel-trends assumptions, the latter allowing MTP effects to be studied with some unobserved confounding, and the point of using SNMMs is to characterize time-varying HETEROGENEITY of MTP effects.
overlap_with_us: This is the exact template for our (i) if we frame a user turn as a modification of the prompt the user would naturally have written: SNMM/blip machinery under MTP-style interventions in a general time-varying setting, including a route that tolerates unobserved confounding. Treatments are conventional (continuous/multivariate), not language-valued; no text, no estimation with neural nuisances, no policy learning.

title: Studying continuous, time-varying, and/or complex exposures using longitudinal modified treatment policies
venue_date: arXiv 2023-04-19 (Diaz and co-authors; the LMTP methodology line, with arXiv:2006.01366 the nonparametric LMTP paper and arXiv:2508.11131 a 2025-08 extension to rates of change)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED by arXiv listing title/id match; I did not open the abs page, so treat the id as verified and the details as drawn from the surrounding literature. LMTPs are the unified framework for causal effects of complex, continuous, multivariate, and time-varying exposures, generalizing shift, threshold, and stochastic interventions where the natural population- or individual-level exposure value is modified, and they are the standard answer to limited overlap and practical positivity violations, grace periods, and longitudinal settings with censoring and competing risks.
overlap_with_us: This is the single most useful unclaimed transfer for our (i): LMTPs solve exactly the positivity problem that kills 'set the prompt to p' interventions, and the natural-value-of-exposure device is how one legitimately intervenes on a prompt a user would have written anyway. I found NO paper applying LMTPs or incremental-propensity-score interventions to text-valued or embedding-valued exposures, so 'LMTP-style stochastic shift interventions on the user's prompt' looks genuinely open.

title: Doubly Robust Fusion of Many Treatments for Policy Learning
