venue_date: arXiv v1 2025-05-12, v2 2025-05-24; accepted ICML 2025 (Ke Zhu, Jianing Chu, Ilya Lipkovich, Wenyu Ye, Shu Yang)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED. Tackles individualized treatment rules when there are MANY treatment groups, where data are sparse within groups and covariate distributions are badly unbalanced across groups. Proposes a calibration-weighted treatment FUSION procedure that balances covariates and fuses similar treatments through a penalized working model, recovering latent treatment-group structure if either the calibration or the outcome model is right; then standard ITR learners (e.g. policy trees) run in the fused treatment space. Provides consistency, an oracle property for fusion, and regret bounds; applied to a CLL/SLL EHR database.
overlap_with_us: The policy-learning-side answer to a huge action space: fuse near-equivalent actions, then learn the rule in the reduced space — a credible alternative to our plan of optimizing in embedding space for (ii). Single-stage ITR, finite (if many) treatment arms, clinical covariates, no language and no sequence.

title: CausalRM: Causal-Theoretic Reward Modeling for RLHF from Observational User Feedbacks
venue_date: arXiv 2026-03-19, cs.LG/cs.AI/cs.CL/stat.ML; no venue listed (Hao Wang, Licheng Pan, Zhichao Chen, Chunyuan Zheng, Zhixuan Chu, Xiaoxi Li, Yuan Lu, Xinggao Liu, Haoxuan Li, Zhouchen Lin)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED. Introduces 'observational reward modeling' — learning reward models from logged user feedback such as clicks, copies, and upvotes instead of costly controlled annotation — and identifies two problems: annotation noise, and selection bias because users preferentially give feedback on responses they feel strongly about, creating train/inference distribution shift. Fixes noise with a noise-aware surrogate loss provably equivalent to the primal loss under noise-free conditions, and fixes selection bias by reweighting with PROPENSITY SCORES for the probability of a user giving feedback at all. Reports 49.2% gain on WildGuardMix and 32.7% on HarmBench downstream.
overlap_with_us: Nearest published instance of 'a propensity-corrected critic learned from observational human-LLM interaction logs', which is the data regime our causal critic in (iii) will live in. It corrects selection into FEEDBACK, not confounding of the language treatment itself, is single-turn preference modeling, and has no sequential estimand or regime. Related but weaker cousins: arXiv:2601.21350 (factored causal representation for reward models), arXiv:2501.09620 (causal rewards against reward hacking).

title: Text Rationalization for Robust Causal Effect Estimation (CATR)
venue_date: arXiv 2025-12-05, cs.LG; no venue listed (Lijinghua Zhang, Hengrui Cai)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED. Addresses the fact that representing massive text in a feature space routinely violates the positivity assumption at the observational level, because redundant or spurious textual features inflate dimensionality and produce extreme propensity scores, unstable weights, and inflated variance. Proposes Confounding-Aware Token Rationalization, selecting a sparse NECESSARY subset of tokens via a residual-independence diagnostic chosen to retain enough confounding information for unconfoundedness. Demonstrated on synthetic data and MIMIC-III.
overlap_with_us: Text-as-CONFOUNDER rather than text-as-treatment, so it does not compete, but it is the concrete tool for the practical positivity problem our (i) will hit when the conversation history is the time-varying confounder. No sequence, no policy, no STOP.

title: Why Prompt Optimization Works, and Why It Sometimes Doesn't: A Causal-Inspired Edit-Level Analysis
venue_date: arXiv 2026-05-26, cs.CL/cs.LG/cs.NE, 17 pages (Shuzhi Gong, Hechuan Wen)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED, but note the paper is careful to call itself 'causal-inference-INSPIRED observational analysis' using 'propensity-adjusted ASSOCIATIONAL analysis' — any citation claiming it estimates causal effects of prompt edits would be overstated. It studies why optimized prompts from DSPy/TextGrad fail to transfer across benchmarks and backbones, using multiple representations of prompt EDITS. Finds complexity-increasing and meta-instructional edits negatively associated with mathematical and multi-hop reasoning, while step-by-step and meta-cognitive edits help logical and sequential reasoning, robust across cognitive-load annotations, surface features, and edit-motif analyses.
overlap_with_us: Useful as evidence that prompt-edit effects are heterogeneous and task-conditioned — i.e. that our blip functions should be effect-modified by task state — and as a foil, since it explicitly stops short of identification. No sequence, no estimand, no policy.

title: Near-Equivalent Q-learning Policies for Dynamic Treatment Regimes
venue_date: arXiv 2026-03-19, methodology/statistics (Sophia Yazzourh, Erica E. M. Moodie)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED. Extends Q-learning for retrospective DTR data with a worst-value tolerance hyperparameter epsilon giving the maximum acceptable deviation from the optimal expected value, so instead of one optimal action per stage it returns SETS of epsilon-optimal policies. Technically this moves backward recursion from vector-valued to matrix-valued Q representations so multiple admissible value functions coexist, and it explicitly identifies regions of treatment INDIFFERENCE where several decisions give comparable outcomes. Illustrated on a single-stage indifference-boundary example and a simulated multi-stage oncology model with tumor size and toxicity.
overlap_with_us: Directly relevant to two problems our (ii) will face: with a language action space almost all actions are near-equivalent, and the STOP decision is precisely an indifference question (stop when continuing is within epsilon of optimal). Clinical, finite action sets, no text, no generative policy.

title: VCNet and Functional Targeted Regularization For Learning Causal Effects of Continuous Treatments
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED by arXiv listing title/id match only — I did not open the abs page, so treat details as literature-derived. VCNet is a varying-coefficient neural network for the average dose-response function under a CONTINUOUS treatment, using B-spline basis expansion so the estimated ADRF stays continuous in the dose, and it generalizes targeted regularization to get a doubly robust estimator of the whole curve. It is the standard fix for DRNet-style architectures that discretize the treatment into interval-specific heads and thereby lose sensitivity to the dose.
overlap_with_us: Background only, but it is the reference architecture if we parameterize a prompt's effect as a dose-response along a continuous direction in embedding space (the same move CausalCollab's ISE makes). Single-stage, scalar treatment, no text and no sequence.

title: Causal Inference for Human-Language Model Collaboration
venue_date: NAACL 2024 Main Conference; arXiv v1 2024-03-30 (Bohan Zhang, Yixin Wang, Paramveer S. Dhillon)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (id and title match; venue confirmed in arXiv comment field). This is the closest existing instantiation of our setup. It indexes turns t=1..T, defines A_it as "the refinement action performed by user i at time t", treats the LM's accumulated responses L̄_it as the time-varying confounder, assumes sequential exchangeability ("L̄_it, Ā_{i,t-1} capture all confounders at time t"), and explicitly uses the sequential g-formula; their Theorem 1 extends g-computation to functional interventions on a style function f_t(·), with Monte Carlo approximation. The estimand is NOT an ATE but the Incremental Stylistic Effect (ISE), a trajectory-level derivative: the limit as δ→0 of the effect of shifting every turn's text by δ along a style dimension. They deliver CausalCollab for confounding-bias reduction and evaluate on CoAuthor (1,445 human-GPT-3 writing sessions), Baize (1,260 dialogues), and DIALOCONAN (1,200 counter-narrative dialogues). Crucially they state the limitation themselves: "Our work purely estimates the effectiveness of existing strategies, as opposed to directly finding optimal collaboration strategies."
overlap_with_us: Scoops the framing of component (i) almost exactly: user-side text at each turn = time-varying treatment, conversation/LM history = time-varying confounder, final rated quality = outcome, sequential g-formula for identification. Does NOT cover: blip/Q (SNMM-style) decomposition of per-turn effects, the raw language-valued action (they collapse the treatment to a scalar style function f_t, which is a huge dimension reduction we would not want to concede), optimal regime learning, a STOP action, or any generative policy. Our differentiation must be stated in terms of (a) estimand granularity (per-turn blip vs. trajectory-level incremental style derivative), (b) treatment richness, and (c) components (ii) and (iii), which they explicitly disclaim.

title: Policy Learning with a Natural Language Action Space: A Causal Approach
venue_date: arXiv preprint only, v1 2025-02-24, no updated version and no journal-ref/comment field as of today — apparently still unpublished (same authors: Bohan Zhang, Yixin Wang, Paramveer S. Dhillon)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (id and title match). The follow-up to 2404.00207, and the closest methodological competitor to our components (ii) and (iii). It sets up stages t=1..T with H_t=(L̄_t, Ā_{t-1}), states the Bellman recursion Q_t(H_t,A_t)=E[max_{a_{t+1}} Q_{t+1}(H_{t+1},ā_{t+1})|H_t,A_t], and estimates Dynamic Treatment Regimes with a SINGLE model: Q-learning is run in the T5 encoder representation space by fitting a text classifier on the embedding, then the optimal language action is obtained by gradient ascent on the embedding and decoded back to text via a T5 model trained on a "Repeat [TEXT]" objective. Evaluated on mental-health intervention (ChatGPT-simulated PHQ-9 trajectories), hate-speech countering, and sentiment transfer with T=2. Three important caveats the summaries circulating about this paper understate: the action is the LM's/system's refinement (A_t is "the post-refinement text"), NOT the user's message — the user input L_t is the state; the horizon is fixed at T=2 with no stopping rule or adaptive horizon; and although it invokes potential outcomes Y_T(a_1,...,a_T) and claims to find "LM actions that have a large causal effect", it never states sequential ignorability or any formal identification condition.
overlap_with_us: Overlaps (ii) DTR/Q-learning over language-valued actions and (iii) generating the action by optimizing against the learned critic — which is very nearly our "generative prompt policy trained against a causal critic", just implemented as embedding gradient ascent + decoder rather than a trained generator. Does NOT cover: the STOP action / variable-length horizon (they are fixed-T=2), formal identification of the blip/Q under time-varying confounding (no assumptions stated, which is our opening), and the treatment side is system-side refinement rather than user-side prompt/feedback. It is a preprint with no venue, so we can plausibly claim priority on the identification theory if we move.

title: From Reasoning to Agentic: Credit Assignment in Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models
venue_date: arXiv cs.CL, v1 2026-04-10, v3 2026-08-09; 50 pages, single author Chenchen Zhang; survey/position
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (id and title match). Nominally a 50-page survey of credit assignment in LLM RL, but it contains actual identification results that bear directly on our estimand. Section 2.4 ("Identification Results and the CA-ID Card") gives Proposition 1 (Restored-State Identification), establishing when paired return differences identify a causal contrast under state restoration, and Proposition 2 (Text-Only Non-Identifiability), showing that "even the sign of causal credit need not be identified from (h_u, a_u, R)" without restoration or valid observational assumptions. It defines four evidence tiers — restored-interventional, observational-causal (requiring exchangeability and positivity), model-relative counterfactual, and predictive/proxy — and Section 2.3 names transition non-closure and partial observability as identification barriers. It does not use the terms dynamic treatment regime, g-formula, ATE, or off-policy evaluation.
overlap_with_us: This is the paper most likely to be thrown at our identification section in review. It has already published (as propositions, in a widely-read survey) the negative result that turn-level causal credit in multi-turn LLM trajectories is not identified from logged text alone without exchangeability + positivity or state restoration — which is precisely the assumption set our blip/Q identification will rest on. We must cite it and position our contribution as the constructive sequential-causal version (blip functions, g-formula, optimal regime) of what it states as an abstract identifiability boundary, and its exchangeability/positivity tier is where our sequential ignorability assumption lives.

title: Causal methods for LLM development and evaluation
venue_date: Published at KDD 2026; arXiv 2026-05-25; large multi-author group (Frauen, Brockschmidt, Hess, ... Krishnan, Feuerriegel)
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (id and title match). A published survey/position paper arguing that causal inference is underused across the LLM pipeline (pretraining, alignment, routing, evaluation). It proposes no estimator. Critically for us, Section 3.3.3 names our exact framing in print: it treats "the prompt as treatment and the final outcome as reward", observes that "naive prediction of observed reward does not identify the counterfactual utility of alternative texts", and concludes "This makes the problem a natural instance of off-policy evaluation and policy learning". Section 3.3.2 adds that in agent workflows "their actions influence subsequent states, observations, and ultimately long-term rewards" and that "such sequential decision-making problems are complicated in terms of identifiability and estimation because earlier system choices influence later observations". It does not mention dynamic treatment regimes, time-varying confounding, the g-formula, or multi-turn conversation specifically.
overlap_with_us: Cuts both ways. Bad: a KDD 2026 paper has already articulated "prompt as treatment, outcome as reward, hence OPE + policy learning", so we cannot present that framing as novel. Good: it states it as an open opportunity with no method, and never reaches time-varying confounding or DTRs — so it is the strongest available citation for "the field has named this problem and not solved it". Use it in the intro as the gap statement.

title: Exact Is Easier: Credit Assignment for Cooperative LLM Agents (method name: C3)
venue_date: arXiv cs.LG, v1 2026-03-06, v2 2026-05-08 (Yanjun Chen, Yirong Sun, Hanlin Wang, Jinghan Wang, Xinming Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen, Wenjie Li, Wei Zhang)
what_it_does: STATUS: MISMATCH on the circulating title — secondary sources (a GitHub awesome-list and a search summary) cite 2603.06859 as "C3: Contextual Counterfactual Credit Assignment for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in LLM Collaboration"; the id actually resolves to "Exact Is Easier: Credit Assignment for Cooperative LLM Agents", whose method is named C3. Do not cite the circulating title. What it actually does: argues that agent-removal, learned critics, and trajectory baselines all distort measured contributions, then makes the identification argument that LLM interaction histories contain no hidden state, so exact counterfactuals are available without approximation. C3 "fix[es] the complete history at each decision point, sampl[es] alternative actions under a frozen behavior policy, and comput[es] unbiased per-decision advantages through a parameter-free leave-one-out baseline." Evaluated on math reasoning and code generation, across multi-agent topologies and multi-turn interaction.
overlap_with_us: The "no hidden state in the text history, therefore the per-decision counterfactual is exactly identified by re-sampling under a frozen behavior policy" argument is a direct rival to our sequential-ignorability-plus-g-formula story, and it is a cheaper argument. We need a response: it holds only when the researcher controls the rollout (interventional/restored-state regime), and collapses for logged human-user data where the user's next message is not resamplable and the human's latent intent is an unmeasured confounder. That is exactly our setting and should be made explicit.

title: Prompt Optimization with Logged Bandit Data
venue_date: arXiv 2025-04-03 (cs.LG/cs.AI/cs.IR/stat.ML); Haruka Kiyohara, Daniel Yiming Cao, Yuta Saito, Thorsten Joachims
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (id and title match). Takes the action space to be natural-language prompts and the reward to be logged user feedback (clicks), and notes that naive policy gradient is either high-variance (IPS-style) or biased (reward-model-style). Proposes a kernel-based off-policy gradient estimator that exploits similarity among the generated sentences to cut variance at controlled bias, benchmarked on personalized movie-description generation. It is a single-step contextual bandit: one prompt, one output, one reward — no sequence of actions, no time-varying confounder, no notion of history.
overlap_with_us: Owns the single-step version of our off-policy machinery for language-valued actions, including the variance problem that large text action spaces create. This is the paper a reviewer will cite to ask "why not just contextual bandits?" Our answer is exactly the sequential structure: history as a treatment-affected confounder, per-turn blips, and a STOP decision. Worth citing as the degenerate T=1 case of our estimand.

title: Causal Inference with Generative Artificial Intelligence: Application to Texts as Treatments
venue_date: arXiv stat.AP, v1 2024-10-01, v5 2026-06-11; Kosuke Imai, Kentaro Nakamura
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (id and title match). Targets the ATE when the treatment is an unstructured high-dimensional text. The key move is to have an LLM GENERATE the treatment texts, so the true internal representation that produced them is known; that known representation is then used to separate the treatment feature of interest (sentiment, topic) from confounding textual features, which the authors argue gives nonparametric identification and "eliminates the need to learn causal representation from the data." Extended to a text-reuse setting where an LLM regenerates existing texts. Strictly single-shot: one text treatment, one outcome, no sequence.
overlap_with_us: This is the state of the art for identifying the effect of a language-valued treatment at one time point, and it is the foundation our per-turn blip identification has to build on or argue against. Their trick (known generative representation) is available to us only if we generate the prompts ourselves; for logged human conversations we inherit exactly the latent-representation problem they sidestep. Not a scoop — there is no sequence and no regime — but our identification section is incomplete without engaging it.

title: What if LLMs Ate Their Words: Causal History Effects in Multi-Turn Interaction
venue_date: arXiv, 2026-09-05 (two weeks old); 11 pages, 6 figures, code/data on GitHub; Jinnan Li, Zheren Fu, Yue Wang, Jinzhe Li, Yuan Wu, Yi Chang
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (id and title match; genuinely recent, not a hallucination). Asks whether the assistant's own prior responses causally drive multi-turn degradation. Manipulates assistant-generated history retrospectively via "neutralization" (replacing prior assistant turns with neutral content) and "turn surgery" (intervening on a single assistant turn), replaying the observed user messages against the edited history across 2,973 trajectories, and measures min-max normalized performance change. Finds history effects that "simple context shortening is insufficient to explain". No DTR, no g-formula, no blip functions, no policy learning — the manipulated variable is the ASSISTANT's history, not the user's message.
overlap_with_us: Adjacent but strategically important: it supplies the empirical evidence that conversation history is a genuine causal driver of later task quality, which is precisely the premise behind treating history as a time-varying (and treatment-affected) confounder. It also occupies the phrase "causal history effects in multi-turn interaction", so we should cite it as motivation and be clear our treatment is the user-side turn while theirs is the assistant-side history.

title: Compared to What? Baselines and Metrics for Counterfactual Prompting
venue_date: COLM 2026; arXiv v1 2026-05-01, v2 2026-08-20; Zihao Yang, Mosh Levy, Yoav Goldberg, Byron C. Wallace
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (id and title match; venue COLM 2026). Argues that counterfactual prompting experiments are uninterpretable without a paraphrase baseline, because every text edit is a compound treatment bundling the target variable with incidental surface-form variation (the treatment-variation-irrelevance problem). Empirically, flipping patient gender on MedPerturb changes predictions 14.9% of the time while meaning-preserving paraphrase changes them 14.1% — so many previously reported prompt effects vanish once general model sensitivity is accounted for. Proposes a testing framework comparing target interventions against paraphrase-induced change. Single-turn.
overlap_with_us: Not a competitor, but a live threat to our measurement validity that reviewers will raise: if a per-turn blip is estimated by contrasting one user message against another, we are estimating a compound treatment effect, and the paraphrase-null may swamp the signal. We should pre-empt it by defining the per-turn treatment at the level of an intervention on a specified aspect of the message (with a paraphrase-matched reference level), and cite this paper for doing so.

title: Offline Policy Evaluation of Multi-Turn LLM Health Coaching with Real Users
venue_date: NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Multi-Turn Interactions in Large Language Models; arXiv v1 2025-10-20, v2 2025-10-21; Melik Ozolcer, Sang Won Bae
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (id and title match). Deploys a tool-augmented LLM health coach on the web with real users and does offline policy evaluation over 280 rated dialogue turns from seven participants. Policies are defined over factorized decision heads (Tool / Style) rather than over raw language, plus a lightweight simulator with hidden user archetypes. Headline finding: a policy that maximizes average tool use harms a specific segment (lower health literacy, higher self-efficacy). The abstract does not name specific OPE estimators, and n=7 participants makes it a pilot.
overlap_with_us: The closest thing to an applied precedent for OPE of a multi-turn LLM interaction policy with real users, so it is the natural related-work anchor for our empirical section. It does not threaten us: the action is a low-cardinality decision head rather than a language-valued treatment, there is no time-varying-confounding adjustment, no blip/Q estimand, no STOP action, and the sample is tiny.

title: Causal Discovery and Counterfactual Reasoning to Optimize Persuasive Dialogue Policies
venue_date: arXiv cs.CL, 2025-03-19, 21 pages, 8 figures; Donghuo Zeng, Roberto Legaspi, Yuewen Sun, Xinshuai Dong, Kazushi Ikeda, Peter Spirtes, Kun Zhang
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (id and title match). Multi-turn persuasive dialogue where user strategies are the state and system utterance strategies are the action. Runs the GRaSP causal-discovery algorithm to recover causal relations among user and system utterance strategies, uses a BiCoGAN to generate counterfactual utterances conditioned on the discovered causal factors, and trains a Dueling Double DQN on the augmented data to pick system utterances. So it is causal-discovery-plus-counterfactual-augmentation feeding an RL policy, not identification and estimation of a sequential causal effect.
overlap_with_us: Adjacent: multi-turn, language-mediated, policy-learning, with causal vocabulary — a reviewer may ask how we differ. The distinction is sharp and defensible: their actions are discrete strategy LABELS (not language-valued treatments), the counterfactuals are generative data augmentation rather than identified estimands, and there is no adjustment for time-varying confounding and no target estimand at all.

title: CaRT: Teaching LLM Agents to Know When They Know Enough
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (title matches the id as listed on arXiv). Addresses when an agent should stop gathering information and act, noting that off-the-shelf LLMs poorly estimate their own probability of success even in simple settings, so optimal termination fails. Trains LLMs on counterfactual examples paired with explicit reasoning for termination in multi-step tasks. This is supervised/counterfactual-example training for a stop decision, with no causal estimand, no confounding adjustment, and no off-policy evaluation.
overlap_with_us: The only paper I found that directly targets a learned STOP decision in a multi-turn LLM setting, so it is the incumbent on our component (ii) STOP action. It is not a causal paper, which is the whole gap: we can frame the STOP action as a terminal option inside an optimal dynamic regime with an identified value, versus their behavior-cloning-style approach. Cite it and differentiate on estimand, not on the idea of stopping.

title: Stop Listening to Me! How Multi-turn Conversations Can Degrade LLM Reliability
venue_date: arXiv cs.CL, v1 2026-03-12, v3 2026-05-26; Kevin H. Guo, Chao Yan, Avinash Baidya, Katherine Brown, Xiang Gao, Juming Xiong, Zhijun Yin, Bradley A. Malin
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (id and title match). Introduces a "stick-or-switch" framework, evaluates 17 LLMs on three clinical benchmarks, and reports a "conversation tax" of up to 30% accuracy loss plus "blind switching" — models adopt user suggestions at near-identical rates whether or not the suggestion is correct. The user-side manipulation is a sequential presentation strategy (partitioning the answer space across turns and injecting suggestions). Purely an empirical benchmark; no intervention-based estimand, no identification.
overlap_with_us: Pure motivation, not competition, and useful to us: it documents that user-side turns have large and sign-indeterminate effects on final quality, which is the single best empirical argument that per-turn prompt effects are worth estimating rather than assumed positive. It also strengthens the case for a STOP action (more turns can be actively harmful).

title: The March–August 2026 turn-level credit assignment cluster: Hindsight Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon LLM Agents; Counterfactual Credit Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent Collaboration; TCPO: Turn-Level Credit Policy Optimization
venue_date: All arXiv preprints: 2603.08754 submitted 2026-03-07 (Tan, Yang, Chen, Shao, Wen, Shen, Luo, Du, Guo, Li); 2603.21563 submitted 2026-03-23, v5 2026-06-11 (Zhongyi Li, Wan Tian, Jinju Chen, Huiming Zhang, Yang Liu, Yikun Ban, Fuzhen Zhuang); 2608.01667 submitted 2026-08
what_it_does: STATUS: all three ids CONFIRMED to exist and resolve to the stated titles (I verified 2603.08754 and 2603.21563 directly; 2608.01667 resolves to "TCPO: Turn-Level Credit Policy Optimization"). HCAPO integrates hindsight credit assignment into LLM agents to improve Q-value estimation under sparse long-horizon rewards, using a retrospective LLM critic with counterfactual continuations. CCPO converts joint outcomes into agent-specific signals by estimating each agent's marginal contribution via counterfactual trajectories with the agent's contribution removed, plus a global-history-aware advantage normalization, on top of GRPO/GSPO/REINFORCE++. IMPORTANT ACCURACY FLAG: the widely circulating claim (in a GitHub awesome-list and in search summaries) that CCPO "models the trajectory as a structural causal model where each turn's action is a treatment variable and turn-level credit is the ATE via do-calculus" is OVERSTATED — reading the paper, credit is assigned across AGENTS in a multi-agent system, not across conversation turns, the actions are role-decomposed reasoning steps on math benchmarks rather than natural-language messages, and it uses "counterfactual" informally without ATE, SCM, or do-calculus machinery.
overlap_with_us: Collectively they establish that the RL-for-LLM community is converging on retrospective counterfactual credit at the turn/agent level, which is the nearest neighbor to our per-turn blip and will be cited against us as "already done". The rebuttal is concrete: all three assign credit to the SYSTEM's own actions inside a controllable rollout (which is a within-model advantage/variance-reduction problem), none targets an identified causal parameter for an exogenous human-generated message under time-varying confounding, none addresses positivity or a behavior policy we do not control, and none learns an optimal regime with a STOP rule.

title: Causal Agent Replay: Counterfactual Attribution for LLM-Agent Failures
venue_date: arXiv cs.LG, 2026-06-06; single author Jaineet Shah
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (id and title match; genuinely a 2026 paper, not fabricated). Models a single agent execution as a structural causal model and intervenes on individual steps to attribute failure, rather than merely flagging the step that took the harmful action. Provides a single-step contrastive estimator and a budget-bounded Monte-Carlo Shapley estimator with confidence intervals, validated on synthetic SCMs where it recovers pivotal steps and two-step interactions. Open-source, works with hosted or local models.
overlap_with_us: Adjacent: shares the within-trajectory intervention idea and the SCM framing, and shares our concern with multi-step interactions. Not a threat — it is retrospective per-trajectory attribution (Shapley over steps), not population-level estimation of a sequential causal effect, the interventions are on the agent's own steps rather than user messages, there is no regime learning or STOP, and validation is synthetic with a single author and no venue.

title: Distal Causal Excursion Effects: Modeling Long-Term Effects of Time-Varying Treatments in Micro-Randomized Trials
venue_date: Biometrics 2025/2026 (Oxford Academic, vol 81 issue 4, ujaf134, published 2026); arXiv 2025-02-19; companion: Shi, Wu & Dempsey, arXiv:2212.01472
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (id resolves to this title, and it is genuinely published in Biometrics). In micro-randomized trials each participant is sequentially randomized hundreds of times among intervention options (e.g. send vs. do not send a supportive message). The paper introduces the distal causal excursion effect (DCEE), an estimand that quantifies the long-term effect of time-varying treatments by contrasting distal outcomes under two excursion policies while marginalizing over most treatment assignments, closing the gap between MRTs' proximal outcomes and their long-term behavior-change goals.
overlap_with_us: Pure background but methodologically the best-matched estimand template outside NLP: a sequentially delivered MESSAGE as a time-varying treatment with a delayed final outcome, marginalizing over the rest of the treatment path. Our contribution can be positioned as importing this estimand class into language-valued action spaces. The treatments here are binary send/no-send, not language-valued, so there is no scoop risk — and the excursion-effect construction is a useful alternative to a full blip model when positivity over raw text is hopeless.

id: arXiv:1802.02163 (Science Advances 2022) and Fong & Grimmer, AJPS 2023
title: How to Make Causal Inferences Using Texts (Egami, Fong, Grimmer, Roberts, Stewart) / Causal Inference with Latent Treatments (Fong & Grimmer)
venue_date: arXiv 2018-02-06; published Science Advances 2022 (10.1126/sciadv.abg2652). Fong & Grimmer, American Journal of Political Science, 2023
what_it_does: STATUS: CONFIRMED (both resolve; the Science Advances and AJPS publications are real). Egami et al. show that nearly all text-based causal inference depends on a latent representation of the text, that estimating that representation from the same data creates an identification problem or overfitting, and propose a split-sample workflow for using discovered measures as treatments or outcomes. Fong & Grimmer show that randomizing the texts alone does NOT identify the effect of a latent treatment, because other unmeasured textual treatments confound it, and give sufficient conditions plus designs (explicitly adjusting for confounding text features; many-versions-of-the-text designs) to make identification plausible.
overlap_with_us: Background but load-bearing: this is the canonical statement of the problem our per-turn treatment definition inherits, at a single time point. The Fong & Grimmer result — randomization of the text is not enough when the treatment of interest is a latent feature of it — is the hardest obstacle to defining our per-turn treatment, and we need an explicit answer (split-sample, many-versions design, or a generated-treatment design as in Imai & Nakamura 2410.00903). No sequential component, so no competitive risk.

title: Policy Learning with a Natural Language Action Space: A Causal Approach
venue_date: arXiv preprint, cs.CL, submitted 2025-02-24 (v1 only; no published venue found in arXiv metadata, and I could not confirm any conference acceptance). Authors: Bohan Zhang, Yixin Wang, Paramveer S. Dhillon (Michigan).
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED (id and title match; abstract read verbatim). This is explicitly a causal framework for MULTI-STAGE decision-making in natural-language action spaces where the outcome is only observed after a sequence of actions. It uses Q-learning to estimate Dynamic Treatment Regimes (their words) through a single model, does policy learning by gradient ascent on language embeddings, and contributes a decoding strategy that maps optimized embeddings back to coherent natural language. Evaluated on mental-health intervention, hate-speech countering, and sentiment transfer with human eval; pitched as data-efficient vs PPO (which needs policy+value+reward models).
overlap_with_us: This is the closest thing to a direct scoop and it must be confronted head-on in related work. It already covers: (a) language-valued actions as a sequential treatment, (b) Q-learning/DTR estimation of the optimal regime over those actions, and (c) generating language by optimizing against the learned Q (i.e., our 'generative policy against a causal critic' in embryonic form). What it does NOT do, and where our remaining novelty lives: no STOP/termination action; no explicit treatment of the conversation history as a time-varying confounder with sequential-exchangeability / positivity conditions stated and defended; no blip / structural-nested-mean-model formulation and no doubly-robust or g-estimation machinery (single-model plug-in Q-learning only); no inference (no CIs, no sequential-policy-value inference); actions are agent-side utterances in scripted tasks, not the real user's prompt/feedback in an observational human-LLM log. Our positioning should be: they did plug-in Q-learning over embeddings, we do identification + robust estimation + STOP + policy distillation.

title: What is the Causal Effect of a Conversation? Estimands and Inference in AI Mediated Conversations
venue_date: arXiv preprint, stat.ME, submitted 2026-07-03. Authors: Adriane Fresh, Aiden Shin. Political-methodology framing.
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED (abstract read verbatim). Develops a potential-outcomes framework for causal inference when the treatment is a conversation, motivated by GenAI-mediated survey/field experiments. Its core move is to separate six distinct causal objects with distinct estimands and identifying assumptions: assignment to a conversational condition, assignment to a conversational POLICY, opening messages, messages within a conversation, realized conversational features, and the full realized conversation. It argues the post-randomization conversation is endogenous because it is jointly generated by respondent and agent, so randomizing assignment does not identify message-level or feature-level effects; those need 'sequential assumptions, representations of conversational histories, or explicit message-level interventions'. It is a conceptual/estimand paper only: no estimators, no simulations, no policy learning, no g-formula, no blip functions, no stopping.
overlap_with_us: Directly overlaps our contribution (i) at the estimand level, and it plants the flag on exactly our vocabulary ('assignment to a conversational policy', 'message-level interventions', 'representations of conversational histories' = our time-varying confounder). If we do not cite this, a reviewer will read our identification section as unaware of it. The good news is that it stops precisely where we start: they name the sequential-assumption requirement but supply no identification result, no estimator, no optimal-regime learning, and no STOP action. Our framing should shift from 'we formalize prompts as time-varying treatments' to 'we take the message-level estimand that Fresh & Shin show is unidentified by design randomization, give sequential-exchangeability/positivity conditions under which blip/Q functions are identified, and estimate them'.

title: GenAI Powered Dynamic Causal Inference with Unstructured Data
venue_date: arXiv preprint, stat.ME, submitted 2026-05-08, revised 2026-09-15 (v2). Authors: Kentaro Nakamura, Kosuke Imai.
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED. Proposes estimating causal effects of unstructured treatments (text, image, video) where the treatment is a SEQUENCE of features rather than one static object. It extracts internal representations from generative-AI models, then fits a marginal structural model with neural networks while jointly learning a deconfounder for each treatment feature in the sequence, and delivers asymptotically valid confidence intervals. Validated in simulation and applied to a randomized experiment on Hong Kong protests, finding a treatment feature's effect depends critically on its position within the text.
overlap_with_us: This is the strongest methodological overlap with our estimation layer: it is literally a marginal structural model with sequentially-deconfounded, GenAI-embedded, language-valued treatment features, with valid inference, from Imai's group. It covers a lot of our (i)/(ii) machinery. The distinction we must make loudly: their 'sequence' is the ordered features WITHIN one static document, and the conversation is not interactive -- there is no feedback loop where the history is generated jointly with the treatment, no adaptive regime, no policy learning, no STOP. Given Imai's group is actively revising this (v2 in Sept 2026), assume a multi-turn/interactive follow-up is plausible before late 2026; we should differentiate on the adaptive-regime and STOP contributions rather than on 'MSM for language treatments', which is now taken.

title: What if LLMs Ate Their Words: Causal History Effects in Multi-Turn Interaction
venue_date: arXiv preprint, cs.CL + cs.AI, submitted 2026-09-05, 11 pages, code/data released. Authors: Jinnan Li, Zheren Fu, Yue Wang, Jinzhe Li, Yuan Wu, Yi Chang.
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED (id resolves to this exact title). Measures whether an LLM's own prior turns causally shape its later performance in multi-turn conversations. Method is retrospective counterfactual replay ('neutralization' / turn surgery): replay the same user messages on completed SHARDED conversations while editing ONLY the assistant-generated history, e.g. replacing prior assistant responses with neutral content. Across 6 task families, 5 models, 2,973 trajectories they report that assistant history has 'active but selective' effects (reported downstream change of about +.027), and that single-turn-to-multi-turn degradation is task- and model-dependent.
overlap_with_us: Overlaps our conceptual claim that turns in a conversation are interventions and history is the causal carrier -- and it gets the empirical 'history matters causally' result first, with released code and a benchmark-scale trajectory set. It is, however, an interventional-audit paper, not a causal-inference paper: the intervened object is the ASSISTANT's history (not the user's prompt), there is no estimand, no confounding-adjustment, no positivity/exchangeability discussion, no effect estimator with inference, no policy learning, no STOP. CAUTION ON PROVENANCE: a search snippet asserted this is an ICML 2026 accepted paper -- that claim is NOT supported by arXiv metadata and I found no acceptance record, so do not cite it as an ICML paper. Also note the aggregator hosts pith.science circulating this paper are not legitimate primary sources.

title: Optimizing Prompts for Large Language Models: A Causal Approach (Causal Prompt Optimization, CPO)
venue_date: arXiv preprint, submitted 2026-02-02. Authors: Wei Chen, Yanbin Fang, Shuran Fu, Fasheng Xu, Xuan Wei. Information-systems / enterprise framing.
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED (abstract read verbatim). Reframes automatic prompt optimization as causal estimation. Stage 1 learns an OFFLINE CAUSAL REWARD MODEL by applying Double Machine Learning to semantic embeddings of prompts and queries, isolating the causal effect of prompt variation from confounding query attributes (their explicit complaint is that existing APO reward models are 'fundamentally correlational'). Stage 2 uses that debiased reward to guide a cheap search for query-specific prompts without online evaluation. Beats human prompts and SOTA optimizers on math reasoning, visualization and data analytics, with gains concentrated on hard queries; also argued as a cost story (offline causal model instead of online execution).
overlap_with_us: This is our contribution (iii) minus the sequentiality: a causal (DML/CATE) critic trained offline, then used to drive prompt generation, with the query as the confounder. The 'prompt policy trained against a causal critic' idea is therefore no longer novel on its own. Explicitly single-turn per the abstract: no multi-turn, no sequential decision-making, no dynamic treatment regimes, no stopping. Our differentiator has to be the sequential/blip structure (effect of a prompt GIVEN history, with history as a time-varying confounder induced by the earlier prompt) rather than 'we use causal ML instead of a correlational reward model'.

title: The Confounder Trap: Treatment-Encoding Representations in Causal Inference with Text
venue_date: arXiv preprint, stat.ME, submitted 2026-07-28. Authors: Marie Neubrander, Graham Tierney, Alexander Volfovsky (Duke).
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED. Identifies and formalizes 'representation-induced overlap failure': when treatment information is embedded in the text being adjusted for, learned representations encode treatment status and make treated/control documents separable, inducing positivity violations even when the underlying causal problem satisfies overlap. Proposes masking treatment-defining lexical signal before representation learning -- deletion masking for bag-of-words/topic models, replacement masking for LLMs (hide treatment tokens, keep context). Shows masking preserves overlap, stabilizes effect estimates and reduces bias versus unmasked adjustment.
overlap_with_us: Not a scoop, but a paper we cannot afford to ignore and probably our most useful technical ally-plus-threat. Our setup is the worst case for this failure mode: the time-varying confounder (the conversation history) literally CONTAINS the past treatments (the prior prompts), so any embedding of history encodes treatment and our sequential positivity will be attacked on exactly these grounds. Expect a reviewer to cite this at us. We should pre-empt it with an explicit sequential-positivity discussion and a masking or residualization step in the history representation.

title: Causal Effect Estimation with Latent Textual Treatments
venue_date: arXiv preprint, cs.CL, submitted 2026-02-17. Authors: Omri Feldman, Amar Venugopal, Jann Spiess, Amir Feder (Stanford/Columbia).
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED. End-to-end pipeline for generating AND estimating latent textual interventions. Generation phase uses sparse autoencoders to produce controlled text variants that differ in a targeted latent feature; estimation phase applies residualization-based corrections. Its core diagnosis is that naive estimation is badly biased because text inherently conflates treatment and covariate information, and residualization is their fix.
overlap_with_us: Adjacent: single-shot text treatment, no turns, no sequence, no policy. Relevant to us twice over: it is the standard reference for the treatment/covariate conflation problem in text (same issue as the Confounder Trap paper, independently), and its SAE-based generation of controlled language interventions is a plausible competitor mechanism for constructing the language-valued treatment contrasts our blip functions need. Cite it as the single-stage special case of our sequential problem.

title: Exact Is Easier: Credit Assignment for Cooperative LLM Agents (method: C3)
venue_date: arXiv preprint, cs.LG, v1 2026-03-06, v2 2026-05-08. Authors: Yanjun Chen, Yirong Sun, Hanlin Wang, Jinghan Wang, Xinming Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen, Wenjie Li, Wei Zhang.
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED with a title caveat -- the id resolves to this work but the CURRENT arXiv title is 'Exact Is Easier: Credit Assignment for Cooperative LLM Agents', whereas search snippets circulate an older/other title, 'Contextual Counterfactual Credit Assignment for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in LLM Collaboration' (retitled across versions; not a different paper). Argues that because LLM interaction histories are deterministic text records with no hidden state, per-decision causal contributions can be measured EXACTLY rather than approximated: fix the complete history at each decision point, sample alternative actions under a frozen behavior policy, and compute unbiased per-decision advantages with a parameter-free leave-one-out baseline. Evaluated on six math/code benchmarks, two model families, two multi-agent topologies.
overlap_with_us: Adjacent but methodologically uncomfortably close to our blip estimation: 'fix the complete history, resample the action' is precisely conditioning on the time-varying confounder to identify a turn-level contrast, arrived at from the RL side without causal-inference vocabulary. The treatment is agent-to-agent messaging in a cooperative multi-agent system, not a human user's prompt, and there is no time-varying-confounding formalism, no DTR, no STOP, no observational-data story (they can resample at will, we generally cannot). Useful to cite as the 'you can just replay' baseline and to explain why observational human logs break that luxury.

title: Causal Agent Replay: Counterfactual Attribution for LLM-Agent Failures
venue_date: arXiv preprint, cs.LG + cs.AI, submitted 2026-06-06. Author: Jaineet Shah. Open-source implementation released.
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED. Models an LLM agent run as a structural causal model and applies a do-operation to an individual step to attribute failure. Contributes an intervention algebra over agent steps, a single-step contrastive estimator, and a budget-bounded Monte-Carlo Shapley estimator that divides credit among interacting steps. Purely post-hoc attribution/debugging; the abstract mentions no time-varying confounding, no g-computation, no dynamic treatment regimes and no policy learning.
overlap_with_us: Adjacent. Shares the 'a step in a trajectory is an intervention' premise and the SCM/do-operator apparatus, so it competes for the same conceptual real estate, but it answers 'which step broke this run' rather than 'what is the sequential effect of a language intervention and what is the optimal adaptive regime'. No stopping, no regime, no user-side treatment. Cite as attribution-not-policy prior work.

title: Counterfactual Credit Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent Collaboration (CCPO / SEPO)
venue_date: arXiv preprint, cs.AI, v1 2026-03-23, revised through v5 2026-06-11. Authors: Zhongyi Li, Wan Tian, Jinju Chen, Huiming Zhang, Yang Liu, Yikun Ban, Fuzhen Zhuang.
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED (id and title match; abstract read verbatim). Two optimizer-agnostic credit-assignment methods that turn a shared terminal reward into agent-specific signals for multi-agent LLM RL: CCPO estimates an agent's marginal contribution by comparing the realized joint outcome to a counterfactual where that agent is removed; SEPO uses constrained self/peer evaluation as a verifier-anchored signal. Both operate at the reward-construction layer feeding GRPO/GSPO/REINFORCE++, instantiated in a sequential Think--Solve setting on math benchmarks, with gains that vary by model and dataset.
overlap_with_us: Adjacent only. IMPORTANT PROVENANCE WARNING: secondary sources (an emergentmind topic page, a GitHub 'awesome credit assignment' list) describe CCPO as 'casting each turn action as a treatment in a structural causal model', 'targeting turn-level ATE via do-calculus', and 'theoretical guarantees under no unobserved confounders within the trajectory' -- NONE of that language appears in the actual abstract, which is a leave-one-agent-out reward-shaping paper. Do not cite those characterizations; they appear to be embellished secondary summaries. The real paper is agent-removal credit shaping, no DTR, no confounding formalism, no user-side treatment.

title: The Prompt Is Not the Query: How Request State Evolves Across Multi-Turn AI Conversations
venue_date: arXiv preprint, submitted 2026-07-24. (Verified via the arXiv API, which is authoritative for id/title/date; I have only the API's one-line abstract summary, not the full text.)
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED for id/title/date; description is thin. Empirical study showing that in multi-turn AI conversations the conversation history contains substantial request-relevant information that is absent from the final prompt, i.e. the latest user message is not a sufficient statistic for what the user is actually asking. No causal-inference machinery indicated.
overlap_with_us: Not a threat; genuinely useful to us. It is the cleanest citable empirical justification for our central modeling choice -- that the current prompt alone is not sufficient and the accumulated history must enter as a time-varying covariate/confounder rather than be marginalized away. Recommend citing it in the motivation, not the related-work-threat section.

title: Causal Methods for LLM Development and Evaluation
venue_date: KDD 2026 (venue stated in arXiv metadata); arXiv submitted 2026-05-25. Authors: Dennis Frauen, Marie Brockschmidt, Konstantin Hess, Haorui Ma, Yuchen Ma, Abdurahman Maarouf, Maresa Schroeder, Jonas Schweisthal, Yuxin Wang, Athiya Deviyani, Sonali Parbhoo, Rahul G. Krishnan, Stefan Feuerriegel.
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED (title, date and KDD 2026 venue). A large-author position/survey paper arguing that causal inference is underused in LLM development despite the questions being inherently causal. Three contributions: how causal methods handle logged data and distribution shift, a map of opportunities across the LLM pipeline (pretraining, alignment, routing, agentic workflows, evaluation), and proposed research directions. The abstract shows no coverage of multi-turn interaction, time-varying treatments, dynamic treatment regimes, or prompts-as-treatments; interventions discussed are pipeline-level (data domains, routing, annotator preferences).
overlap_with_us: Background, but strategically important in two ways. First, it is the agenda-setting citation a reviewer will expect us to engage with, and it is from Feuerriegel's and Krishnan's groups -- exactly the people positioned to publish the multi-turn sequential version next. Second, a survey at a major venue explicitly mapping 'opportunities' here means our gap is publicly flagged as an opportunity; the window is narrower than it looks. Worth checking its agentic-workflows section in full text for whether it already names sequential/multi-turn treatment effects as a direction.

title: Treatment, evidence, imitation, and chat
venue_date: arXiv preprint, stat.OT + cs.AI, submitted 2025-06-29, last revised 2026-04-28, 12 pages. Author: Samuel J. Weisenthal.
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED. A conceptual/position paper distinguishing the 'treatment problem' (choosing an action to optimize an outcome, which requires causal inference) from the 'chat problem' (producing plausible conversational text, solvable by imitation). Its central argument is that imitation alone cannot solve the true treatment problem, though it may still be useful, and it discusses the ethics of experimentation and the assumptions needed for observational data, using statins as a running example.
overlap_with_us: Background, and useful rhetorically: it is the cleanest existing statement of the argument our paper needs in its introduction -- that next-token imitation of good conversations is not the same as learning an optimal regime, so a causal objective is required. No estimands, no estimators, no DTR formalism, no multi-turn treatment structure. Zero scoop risk; high citation value for framing.

title: Are Large Language Models Dynamic Treatment Planners? An In Silico Study from a Prior Knowledge Injection Angle
venue_date: arXiv preprint, cs.LG + cs.CE, submitted 2025-08-06, 20 pages. Authors: Zhiyao Luo, Tingting Zhu (Oxford).
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED. Evaluates open-source LLMs as insulin-dosing agents inside a Type 1 diabetes simulator, comparing zero-shot prompted LLMs against trained neural-network RL agents. Finds that with carefully designed prompts a small model (Qwen2.5-7B) can match trained agents, but documents arithmetic hallucination, temporal misinterpretation and inconsistent clinical logic, and argues for hybrid language-plus-physiological-model approaches before clinical use.
overlap_with_us: Background only, but worth naming to avoid a terminological collision: it puts 'LLM' and 'dynamic treatment' in the same title while doing the OPPOSITE thing -- the LLM is the decision-maker executing a DTR over medical doses, whereas in our setup the language itself is the treatment and the DTR is over prompts. Citing it lets us draw that distinction explicitly rather than have a reviewer accuse us of overclaiming novelty on the phrase.

title: On the Prospects of Dynamic LLM Conversations in Software Development
venue_date: arXiv preprint, cs.SE, submitted 2026-08-31. Authors: Annemarie Wittig, Alina Mailach, Janet Siegmund, Norbert Siegmund.
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED. A longitudinal three-arm experiment with CS students on a full-stack web project: a context-aware arm receiving 'intent-based conversation augmentation', a proactive arm receiving follow-up suggestions and tailored advice, and a control arm with no intervention. Analyzes interaction logs and surveys; reports no detectable harm and only trends toward increased satisfaction in the proactive arm. Descriptive between-arm comparison with no causal-inference machinery, no adaptive per-turn strategy and no policy learning.
overlap_with_us: Background. Its value to us is as an existence proof that randomized conversational-augmentation interventions on real multi-turn developer-LLM sessions are already being run and already producing null/weak results from arm-level comparison. That is the empirical motivation for our estimand argument: assignment-level contrasts wash out heterogeneous per-turn effects, which is exactly why one needs turn-level blip functions and an adaptive regime. Good applied citation, no scoop risk.

title: Why Prompt Optimization Works, and Why It Sometimes Doesn't: A Causal-Inspired Edit-Level Analysis
venue_date: arXiv preprint, cs.CL, submitted 2026-05-26. Authors: Shuzhi Gong, Hechuan Wen.
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED. Asks why automated prompt optimizers (DSPy, TextGrad) fail to generalize across tasks and backbones, by analyzing optimized prompts at the level of individual EDITS using propensity-adjusted associational analysis plus several complementary representations of prompt edits. Finds complexity-increasing and meta-instructional edits are negatively associated with math and multi-hop reasoning performance, while step-by-step and meta-cognitive edits help logical/sequential reasoning. THE SUMMARY IN CIRCULATION IS OVERSTATED: the authors themselves label this 'causal-inspired' and the analysis is propensity-adjusted associational, not formal identification or estimation.
overlap_with_us: Background. Relevant as evidence that edit-level / intervention-level heterogeneity in prompting is real and is being studied, and as a soft target: it is exactly the kind of 'causal-flavored but not identified' analysis our paper can position against. No sequential structure, no regime, no stopping, no estimator with guarantees.

title: Epistemic Regret Minimization: Label-Free Causal Critique Beyond Outcome Reward
venue_date: arXiv preprint, cs.AI, v1 2026-02-12, v4 2026-05-19. Authors: Edward Y. Chang, Longling Geng.
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED. Builds a label-free critic that judges HOW an LLM reasoned rather than only whether the answer was right, flagging and repairing specific reasoning pathologies -- unexamined confounders, correlation/intervention conflation, unchecked back-door paths -- without ground-truth causal graphs or gold answers, and accumulating evidence across episodes into a reward signal. Reports 78-91% recovery for reasoning-heavy models under causal critique versus 25-31% with outcome-only reward, across 1,360 scenarios and six frontier LLMs.
overlap_with_us: Background, and flagged mainly to prevent a naming collision. Its 'causal critique' critiques the MODEL'S causal reasoning; our 'causal critic' is an estimated causal-effect function (blip/Q) used as a training signal. Different objects entirely. We should avoid the phrase 'causal critique' in our title/abstract so as not to be conflated with this line of work.

title: CIVeX: Causal Intervention Verification for Language Agents
venue_date: arXiv preprint, cs.AI, submitted 2026-05-09. Author: Fabio Rovai.
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED, though I would treat the reported results with caution (single author, strong claims). Argues that a schema-valid tool call is not a valid intervention: existing guards (validators, policy filters, provenance checks, self-verification) never certify that a state-changing action has an IDENTIFIABLE causal effect. Maps proposed actions to causal queries on action-state graphs, checks identifiability, and returns EXECUTE / REJECT / EXPERIMENT / ABSTAIN with assumption-scoped certificates carrying identification arguments and confidence bounds. Claims zero false executions under adversarial conditions and large margins over baselines including chain-of-thought verifiers.
overlap_with_us: Background/adjacent. It is the only paper I found that makes IDENTIFIABILITY itself the operative criterion for an agent action, which rhymes with our identification-first stance, and its EXPERIMENT/ABSTAIN verdicts are a distant cousin of our STOP action. But the setting is tool-call safety on action-state graphs, not sequential effects of language interventions on task quality, and there is no time-varying confounding, no regime learning, no outcome model.

title: Active Causal Experimentalist (ACE): Learning Intervention Strategies via Direct Preference Optimization
venue_date: arXiv preprint, cs.LG, v1 2026-02-02, v2 2026-06-18. Authors: Patrick Cooper, Alvaro Velasquez.
what_it_does: STATUS CONFIRMED. Learns experimental design as a sequential policy for causal DISCOVERY. Key observation: absolute information gains shrink as knowledge accumulates, destabilizing value-based RL, but relative comparisons between candidate interventions stay meaningful -- so they train with DPO on pairwise intervention comparisons instead of non-stationary reward magnitudes. Reports 70-71% improvement over random/greedy-infogain/round-robin baselines at equal budget, and the learned policy rediscovers that collider mechanisms need concentrated interventions on parents.
overlap_with_us: Background. Same abstract shape as our (ii)+(iii) -- learn an adaptive sequential intervention policy, train it with a preference/policy-optimization objective -- but the interventions are do-operations on structured variables for graph discovery, not natural language, and the objective is information gain about a graph, not a task-quality outcome under a fixed causal structure. Worth citing as adjacent 'adaptive intervention policy' work, and it is a useful precedent for the argument that relative/preference training is more stable than value regression, which may matter for our policy-distillation step.
